ScenarioTitle: This 18-year-old patient is presenting with poor oral hygiene.
Background: This 18-year-old patient is presenting with poor oral hygiene. The patient is showing early signs of gum disease. It looks like he/she has been eating a lot of sugar and he/she has a history of dry mouth and hay fever (allergic rhinitis). You notice the patient has chewing gum (a type of candy/sweet that is chewed for long periods of time).
TasksJson: ["Find out if the patient is chewing gum, how often he/she is chewing it and if it has sugar.","Inform the patient of the condition of his/her teeth.","Explain that the sugar content of the patient\u0027s gum is contributing to his/her early periodontitis (e.g., high sugar intake leads to heavy plaque build-up, chronic gingival inflammation and eventually early periodontitis, etc.).","Suggest alternatives to chewing sugary gum (e.g. sugar-free gum, drinking water, etc.).","Recommend that the patient see his/her doctor for medication to reduce the symptoms of his/her hay fever."]

ScenarioTitle: You see the parent of a six-year-old boy with bruxism (excessive grinding of the teeth).
Background: You see the parent of a six-year-old boy with bruxism (excessive grinding of the teeth). The parent would like some advice. The child is not present.
TasksJson: ["Find out reason for parent\u2019s visit.","Explore details about child\u2019s bruxism (onset, frequency, previous occurrences, family history, etc.). Find out other relevant information about child (any snoring, poor sleep, irritability/restlessness throughout day, etc.).","Give information about bruxism (e.g., sleep-related movement disorder: reflex, common, etc.). Describe possible problems linked to bruxism (headaches, earaches, tooth damage, etc.). Explore relevance of these to child.","Describe ways of dealing with bruxism (e.g., splint/mouth guard: moulded to fit child\u2019s teeth, worn at night; sleep hygiene: set bedtime, staying hydrated, dark room/no lights; etc.). Recommend next steps (e.g., initial appointment for child: checking damage to teeth, evaluating need for treatment; regular appointments to monitor; etc.). Find out any other questions/concerns.","Reassure parent about bruxism (e.g., often self-limiting with onset of adult teeth, recent onset: damage unlikely, etc.). Establish parent\u2019s willingness to bring child in for appointment."]

ScenarioTitle: Your 30-year-old patient is presenting with a severely ulcerated mouth (ulcerated mucosal surfaces) and sore gingivae.
Background: Your 30-year-old patient is presenting with a severely ulcerated mouth (ulcerated mucosal surfaces) and sore gingivae.
TasksJson: ["Find out details about patient\u2019s sore gums and ulcers (onset, previous occurrences, etc.).","Find out about patient\u2019s dental hygiene practices (brushing, flossing, visits to dentists, etc.).","Give possible causes of mouth ulcers (e.g., bacteria/virus, nutritional deficiency, vigorous brushing, etc.).","Outline treatment (scale/clean, mouthwash, course of antibiotics, topical pain killers if required, etc.).","Explain possible side effects of antibiotics (e.g., nausea, stomach problems, rash, etc.).","Reassure patient about possible side effects (e.g., serious side effects not common, etc.). Establish patient\u2019s consent for examination."]

ScenarioTitle: A patient wants information about dental care during pregnancy, after discovering that she/his wife is about to have their first child.
Background: A patient wants information about dental care during pregnancy, after discovering that she/his wife is about to have their first child. The patient has heard about pregnancy hormones affecting teeth, and that certain dental procedures should be avoided during pregnancy. The couple is anxious to avoid anything that may adversely impact the health of their child.
TasksJson: ["Explain the impact of pregnancy hormones on teeth and gums (e.g., plaque, bleeding gums, infection/inflammation/decay, etc.).","Explain the importance of good oral hygiene to the health of the foetus (e.g., periodontitis linked with premature birth and low birth weight).","Suggest ways to ensure good oral hygiene (e.g., brushing, flossing, antimicrobial mouth rinses, tongue scraping, nutritious meals, etc.).","Answer questions about the risks with amalgam fillings (e.g., mercury vapor, etc.) and antibiotics during pregnancy. Emphasise the importance of avoiding X-rays during first trimester."]

ScenarioTitle: You see a 24-year-old patient who has been getting pain and redness at the back of the lower jaw on the left-hand side.
Background: You see a 24-year-old patient who has been getting pain and redness at the back of the lower jaw on the left-hand side. You have just examined the patient and suspect that the third molar (tooth 38) is impacted (the tooth has failed to emerge fully into its expected position).
TasksJson: ["Find out details about patient\u2019s gum pain (onset, severity, previous occurrences, treatment tried, etc.). Explore any other symptoms (e.g., headaches, unpleasant taste when eating, bad breath, etc.).","Give findings of examination (healthy teeth, no cavities, good oral hygiene, some redness/swelling of gums around lower left molar). Explain impacted tooth as likely cause of gum pain (e.g., insufficient room to develop/emerge, common with onset of wisdom teeth, etc.). Advise need for X-ray (e.g., confirmation of diagnosis, evaluating extent of impaction, assessment of proximity to inferior alveolar nerve canal: risk of nerve damage, etc.).","Advise likely need for extraction (e.g., outpatient procedure: sedation/anaesthetic, removal of tooth; possible referral to specialist; etc.). Find out any concerns.","Warn of risks of delaying treatment (e.g., damage to other teeth/bone, tooth decay, gum disease, development of cyst, etc.).","Make recommendations to ease pain (e.g., over-the-counter pain relief, gargling warm salt water, etc.). Establish patient\u2019s consent for X-ray."]

ScenarioTitle: You see a 22-year-old semi-professional basketball player. He/she has tooth pain from his/her upper left lateral incisor (22).
Background: You see a 22-year-old semi-professional basketball player. He/she has tooth pain from his/her upper left lateral incisor (22). You have just examined the patient; the tooth is loose and has been moved from its original position, with swelling and inflammation of the gums indicating infection.
TasksJson: ["Give findings of examination (infection and damage to tooth, tooth is loose). Find out any patient concerns.","Reassure patient tooth can be saved using root canal therapy (e.g., clearing of infection: repairing damaged inside of tooth, removing dental pulp, filling and sealing space, etc.).","Provide information on alternatives to root canal therapy (e.g., removal of tooth, replacement with implant/denture, etc.). Recommend root canal therapy as best option (e.g., most conservative option, etc.). Find out patient\u2019s reason for not wanting root canal (pain, cost, etc.).","Emphasise need for two additional visits (e.g., X-ray taken today, etc.). Explain steps for visit 1 (e.g., \u2018nerve\u2019 removed, cleaning, enlarging root canal, sealing with temporary filling, etc.). Explain steps for visit 2 (e.g., removing temporary filling, root canal filling inserted, sealed, etc.).","Explain recovery process (e.g., some discomfort, over-the-counter medication, avoiding hard foods, etc.). Establish patient\u2019s consent for X-ray."]

ScenarioTitle: You see a 57-year-old who attended the clinic three weeks ago for a check-up, which was fine.
Background: You see a 57-year-old who attended the clinic three weeks ago for a check-up, which was fine. However, last night he/she bit down hard on a piece of hard food and chipped the upper-right second molar (tooth 17). You have taken an X-ray and have just examined the patient.
TasksJson: ["Find out more details about chipped tooth (when/what happened, any pain, etc.).","Give findings of examination/X-ray (chip to upper-right second molar/tooth 17). Advise need for bonding procedure (e.g., restoration of normal appearance and function, protection of inner layers from irritation/infection, etc.). Outline bonding procedure (e.g., roughening of tooth surface, application of adhesive material, shaping of tooth, hardening with ultra-violet light, etc.). Find out any questions.","Emphasise possible reasons for chipping of tooth (e.g., trauma/injury from biting on hard food, weakened tooth enamel, etc.). Suggest how to avoid chipping teeth (e.g., regular check-ups, avoiding hard foods: popcorn kernels, nuts, ice, etc.). Find out about patient\u2019s oral hygiene (regularity of brushing, use of floss/mouthwash, frequency of tooth cleaning/hygienist appointments, etc.).","Advise patient on oral hygiene (e.g., flossing daily, etc.). Recommend regular hygienist appointments every six months (e.g., deep cleaning, scaling, etc.).","Stress importance of regular hygienist visits (e.g., thorough cleaning, prevention of tooth loss, etc.). Establish patient\u2019s consent to begin bonding procedure."]

ScenarioTitle: You see the parent of an eight-year-old child with a very restricted food range.
Background: You see the parent of an eight-year-old child with a very restricted food range. The parent is worried about nutritional adequacy and has had stressful mealtime experiences.
TasksJson: ["Find out about the child\u0027s accepted foods, drinks, growth information, mealtime behaviour, sensory preferences and any medical/developmental factors already known.","Acknowledge the parent\u0027s concern and explain why pressure and forced feeding can sometimes increase mealtime stress and food refusal.","Explain the principle of gradual exposure and structured, low-pressure opportunities to expand the food range.","Discuss when supplements may be considered and why they should be based on nutritional assessment rather than used automatically.","Agree on a simple home plan and follow-up. Check the parent\u0027s understanding and confidence."]

ScenarioTitle: You see a patient with chronic kidney disease and elevated serum potassium who is reluctant to make dietary changes because the advice feels
Background: You see a patient with chronic kidney disease and elevated serum potassium who is reluctant to make dietary changes because the advice feels restrictive and confusing.
TasksJson: ["Explore the patient\u0027s usual intake and identify the main high-potassium foods and portion patterns relevant to their current diet.","Acknowledge that foods normally considered healthy may need adjustment in some kidney conditions and explain the reason simply.","Explain why elevated potassium can matter even when the patient feels well, without causing unnecessary alarm.","Avoid an overly restrictive approach: discuss portions, frequency, preparation methods and suitable alternatives based on the plan provided by the renal team.","Agree on a small number of priority changes and check that the patient feels able to follow them."]

ScenarioTitle: You are discussing discharge nutrition with a 59-year-old patient after major abdominal surgery.
Background: You are discussing discharge nutrition with a 59-year-old patient after major abdominal surgery. The patient has had poor intake and weight loss but is now medically ready to go home.
TasksJson: ["Acknowledge the patient\u0027s concerns and summarise why nutrition remains important during recovery.","Explain a practical small-and-frequent meal approach and suggest energy/protein-dense options that may be easier to manage.","Discuss the purpose of prescribed oral nutritional supplements and ways to make them more acceptable if appropriate.","Address the likely home situation and suggest how the patient can explain the temporary changes to their spouse or family.","Explain follow-up arrangements and warning signs such as ongoing weight loss or inability to meet intake. Check understanding."]

ScenarioTitle: You see a 46-year-old patient recently diagnosed with type 2 diabetes for an initial dietary consultation.
Background: You see a 46-year-old patient recently diagnosed with type 2 diabetes for an initial dietary consultation.
TasksJson: ["Find out about the patient\u0027s usual eating pattern, meal timing, drinks, portion sizes and main concerns.","Explore previous dieting experience and identify changes the patient feels would be realistic.","Reassure the patient that management does not necessarily mean completely eliminating familiar foods.","Explain the importance of portions, balance and sustainable dietary changes, and correct the misconception that special diabetic foods are automatically required.","Work with the patient to agree on practical initial goals that fit their normal lifestyle. Check understanding and confidence."]

ScenarioTitle: You are reviewing a 38-year-old patient in a weight-management programme.
Background: You are reviewing a 38-year-old patient in a weight-management programme. The patient initially lost 4 kg but has had a six-week weight plateau and is considering a very restrictive diet.
TasksJson: ["Review recent eating patterns, activity, work schedule, sleep and situations in which the plan is hardest to follow.","Acknowledge the patient\u0027s disappointment and explain that plateaus can occur and do not automatically mean failure.","Explore the patient\u0027s belief about metabolism and give a balanced explanation without overpromising.","Discuss the risks and limitations of unsupervised very-low-calorie diets and refocus on sustainable changes.","Agree on a revised plan with measurable goals and a follow-up timeframe. Check motivation and concerns."]

ScenarioTitle: The parent presented two hours ago at the Emergency Department with his/her four-year-old son.
Background: The parent presented two hours ago at the Emergency Department with his/her four-year-old son. The child had a 36-hour history of recurrent vomiting and stomach pain which was diagnosed as viral gastroenteritis. He was given oral re-hydration fluids and observed for two hours. He is now ready to be discharged. The child is not present for your discussion with the parent.
TasksJson: ["Confirm child is ready to be discharged. Find out about parent\u2019s concerns.","Explain viral gastroenteritis (e.g., irritation of stomach or intestines due to viral infection, etc.).","Give information about how gastroenteritis is spread (e.g., contact with vomit/faeces of infected person: shaking hands, contaminated foods/objects, etc.).","Resist request to keep child in hospital (e.g., oral re-hydration therapy usually effective, etc.). Advise on hydration and appropriate clear fluids (e.g., watered down unsweetened fruit juice, electrolyte drinks, etc.). Find out any other concerns.","Advise when to seek medical advice (e.g., signs of severe dehydration: extreme thirst, lethargy, irritability, pale/sunken eyes, etc.)."]

ScenarioTitle: An overweight 76-year-old patient is seeking advice about hip pain.
Background: An overweight 76-year-old patient is seeking advice about hip pain. He/she has experienced worsening pain in the right hip for a number of years. Lately, he/she has begun using a walking stick for support for everyday movements and activity. He/she is anxious about possible reasons for the increased pain and likely treatment recommendations. Be reassuring.
TasksJson: ["Explain possible causes of the symptoms: various, including osteoarthritis (most likely), bursitis, tendinitis, referred pain from back.","Give reasons for the worsening symptoms (e.g., cause remains untreated, etc.).","Inform the patient that hip pain is quite common in people over 65; most common cause is arthritis.","Explain that physical examination and X-ray (for arthritis) are required for diagnosis.","Discuss treatment options: depends on diagnosis (for arthritis \u2013 weight loss, modification of activity, paracetamol, NSAIDs, physiotherapy, referral for hip replacement if conservative treatment fails).","Tell the patient what happens now: diagnostic examination/X-ray; follow-up to confirm diagnosis, treatment plan and treatment monitoring."]

ScenarioTitle: Your patient is a 29-year-old with a tender spot in the lower spine, especially when sitting down.
Background: Your patient is a 29-year-old with a tender spot in the lower spine, especially when sitting down. Recently, he/she has been doing increased training three times weekly for a rowing competition. The patient has come to discuss this with you as the local doctor.
TasksJson: ["Find out about the patient\u0027s pain.","Find out about any recent changes in habits (e.g., at work, leisure time, sport, etc.).","Discuss the likely causes of the patient\u0027s lower back pain (e.g., injury caused by overuse of joints and muscles, can be caused by increasing exercise, etc.).","Give suggestions for treatment (e.g., reduce the exercise regime, consult a physiotherapist, return for further investigation if symptoms persist for more than a month, etc.).","Persuade the patient to follow your recommendations (e.g., it is important to rest from the activity that caused the overuse injury, a physiotherapist can help design a well-balanced training programme, etc.)."]

ScenarioTitle: Your patient is a 52-year-old smoker. Over the last six months, he/she has experienced occasions of breathlessness and chest pain on exertio
Background: Your patient is a 52-year-old smoker. Over the last six months, he/she has experienced occasions of breathlessness and chest pain on exertion. You diagnose angina after asking about the type of pain.
TasksJson: ["Ask the patient to describe the pain.","Explain your diagnosis: angina (reduced blood/oxygen supply to the heart) and reassure the patient that the condition can be effectively managed.","Explain the need to assess other risk factors \u2013 fasting glucose, cholesterol, BP \u2013 and recommend an immediate assessment by a cardiologist.","Caution against strenuous exercise.","Stress the importance of smoking cessation. Offer to discuss ways of helping the patient to quit smoking."]

ScenarioTitle: This 41-year-old patient has been experiencing pain and swelling in the right shoulder.
Background: This 41-year-old patient has been experiencing pain and swelling in the right shoulder. He/she usually plays cricket in his/her spare time, which involves swinging a bat and throwing a ball. You have examined the shoulder and diagnosed bursitis (small fluid-filled sacs usually between the muscles, tendons or bones).
TasksJson: ["Ask when the patient first began experiencing the pain and if the patient injured the shoulder.","Explain why it is unlikely the patient injured the shoulder while playing (e.g., would have felt pain during game, etc.).","Explain your diagnosis and what could have caused the bursitis (e.g., overuse, repeated pressure, etc.).","Persuade the patient to rest the shoulder and not to resume playing cricket until the swelling has gone down.","Suggest other ways to help manage the condition in the long-term (e.g., physiotherapy, joint protection techniques, etc.)."]

ScenarioTitle: You are conducting 15-minute health assessments at a factory workplace.
Background: You are conducting 15-minute health assessments at a factory workplace. A 50-year-old factory worker does not want to cooperate with the assessment because he/she is concerned about the employer having access to his/her medical information. The worker has not had a health check for a long time and is fearful that he/she may have developed diabetes or some other disease. He/she would prefer not to know.
TasksJson: ["Provide reassurance \u2013 work health checks are confidential and provide opportunity to receive immediate feedback and advice on results.","Explain that health checks support a healthier workforce with wide-ranging benefits (e.g., improved productivity, reduced workplace injuries, etc.) plus personal benefits (e.g., individuals learn more about their own health, etc.).","Convince the patient to attend local doctor and undertake testing for diabetes. Explain benefits of risk assessment for preventable disease. Encourage the patient to reduce risk factors (e.g., dietary modification, regular exercise, etc.)."]

ScenarioTitle: Your patient describes two syncopal episodes that have occurred in the last three months.
Background: Your patient describes two syncopal episodes that have occurred in the last three months. The patient has come to see you because he/she is worried that it might happen again. The episodes were not witnessed and you do not know if they were truly syncopal, whether they were convulsions, or even if they were real. You want him/her to see a neurologist.
TasksJson: ["Explain that further investigation is necessary for diagnosis, and that you must do an ECG (electrocardiogram) here in the surgery. You also want to do a CT scan of his/her head and some basic blood tests.","Convince the patient that he/she should visit a neurologist, as a cautionary measure. Reassure him/her and explain what tests the neurologist will run, including an electroencephalogram (EEG).","Without alarming him/her, insist that he/she needs to make time to see the neurologist. Persuade the patient not to drive until the situation is clearer (as any car insurance will not cover the patient in the event of an accident until things are sorted out)."]

ScenarioTitle: This 35-year-old has recently started having difficulty eating foods that contain milk and milk products.
Background: This 35-year-old has recently started having difficulty eating foods that contain milk and milk products. He/she is experiencing stomach cramps and nausea. You suspect secondary lactose intolerance.
TasksJson: ["Question the patient about his/her symptoms (e.g., flatulence, diarrhoea, etc.).","Find out if the patient has experienced any stomach problems (e.g., gastroenteritis) recently.","Explain your diagnosis - secondary lactose intolerance (e.g., gastroenteritis affects lining of gut, etc.).","Respond to the patient\u0027s argument that he/she cannot be lactose intolerant as there is no history of lactose intolerance in the patient\u0027s family (e.g., secondary lactose intolerance not hereditary, etc.).","Discuss when the condition can be expected to subside (e.g., several weeks as the lining of the gut heals, etc.)."]

ScenarioTitle: You are speaking to the parent of a five-year-old girl, Linda, who presents with a barking cough, sneeze and fever.
Background: You are speaking to the parent of a five-year-old girl, Linda, who presents with a barking cough, sneeze and fever. Yesterday you diagnosed mild croup and recommended symptom relief and that the parent seeks medical attention should symptoms worsen. The parent has come to see you again today and is very worried that Linda's condition is getting worse.
TasksJson: ["Ask about Linda\u0027s symptoms.","Suggest steroid treatment.","Explain the possible side-effects of the steroid treatment (e.g., suppression of the immune system, predisposition to infection, etc.).","Reassure the patient that steroids are the best treatment for mild croup and give reasons why (e.g., antibiotic will not eliminate viral infection, etc.).","Offer to review Linda\u0027s case in 24 hours."]

ScenarioTitle: A parent comes in to ask about his/her eight-year-old daughter because he/she has noticed an unusual symptom.
Background: A parent comes in to ask about his/her eight-year-old daughter because he/she has noticed an unusual symptom. Although the child seems well, blood has started appearing in her urine. The parent is concerned, and becomes increasingly anxious as the consultation progresses.
TasksJson:
["Ask the parent about his/her daughter's recent symptoms and general health.","Respond to the parent's concerns. Include the following information:
- Blood in the urine is not a usual symptom for a young child.
- It may not be serious, but is worth investigating.
- It is too soon to say what this symptom might indicate.
- The child will have to have a blood test initially, to be performed immediately.
- The results of the blood test will be available in 24 hours, and the patient should book another appointment as soon as possible to discuss them.
- This symptom could indicate some problem with the child's kidney function.","Be sympathetic and reassuring."]

ScenarioTitle: You are working at a suburban medical clinic. A parent has returned to receive results of an ultrasound performed by his/her 8-year-old daug
Background: You are working at a suburban medical clinic. A parent has returned to receive results of an ultrasound performed by his/her 8-year-old daughter yesterday. The child had presented with vague abdominal pains of several weeks' duration and on examination you felt a right loin mass, which is why you ordered the ultrasound. The ultrasound shows that the child has Wilms' tumour (kidney cancer) and needs to be seen by a specialist urgently.
TasksJson:
["Be sympathetic and reassuring to the parent. Give him/her the following information:

- The results have been received and the news is not good.
- They indicate that the child has kidney cancer (Wilms' tumour).
- This form of kidney cancer is the most common seen in children, and can be effectively treated in most cases, with a good prognosis.
- The child needs to see a specialist (paediatric oncologist) as soon as possible to devise a treatment plan.
- Tell the parent you will arrange an appointment with a specialist straight away."]

ScenarioTitle: Your patient is a music journalist and goes to a lot of live rock concerts.
Background: Your patient is a music journalist and goes to a lot of live rock concerts. The patient has been experiencing tinnitus. He/she felt faint yesterday, but did not lose consciousness. The patient seems very concerned about this.
TasksJson: ["Find out about the patient\u0027s history of tinnitus.","Discuss the possible causes of tinnitus (e.g., exposure to loud noise) and symptoms (e.g., loss of equilibrium/balance, etc.). Explain that the tinnitus could have developed without the patient noticing.","Offer to refer the patient to an ENT (ear, nose, throat) specialist and caution the patient against things that could worsen his/her condition (e.g., loud noise can result in hearing loss, etc.).","Warn the patient that tinnitus may be impossible to cure and stress the importance of protecting the ears from loud music.","Persuade the patient to at least try wearing ear plugs."]

ScenarioTitle: This 65-year-old retired academic opted for early retirement because he/she was finding it difficult to manage his/her workload.
Background: This 65-year-old retired academic opted for early retirement because he/she was finding it difficult to manage his/her workload. There is a fairly strong history of early-onset Alzheimer's disease in his/her family. The patient has come to discuss the possibility of genetic testing with you.
TasksJson: ["Ask the patient if he/she has any questions about dementia generally, and if the patient is familiar with the symptoms of Alzheimer\u0027s.","Discuss the possibility that the patient may be experiencing other forms of impaired cognitive performance, such as depression.","Persuade the patient to see a clinical neuropsychologist before considering having genetic testing and explain the reason for this (e.g., formal cognitive evaluation and assessment of the possibility of depression as a component, etc.).","Explain that prior to any future genetic testing, the patient will need to have specialist genetic counselling (counselling from health professionals with specialist training in genetics and counselling) to consider possible outcomes of the testing."]

ScenarioTitle: Your 49-year-old patient has been recently diagnosed with Hashimoto's thyroiditis, an autoimmune disease which destroys the thyroid gland an
Background: Your 49-year-old patient has been recently diagnosed with Hashimoto's thyroiditis, an autoimmune disease which destroys the thyroid gland and leads to a range of symptoms (including weight gain, depression, fatigue and irregular heart rhythms). The endocrinologist has advised your patient to inform his/her two adult children, as the condition is hereditary. Your patient has some concerns and seeks your advice.
TasksJson: ["Reassure the patient that his/her medical records remain confidential. As the condition is neither life-threatening nor preventable, disclosure is not urgent or enforceable.","Encourage disclosure and give reasons (e.g., careful lifestyle management might prevent early onset; disclosure ensures accurate diagnosis at onset of illness).","Reassure the patient \u2013 you cannot advise on insurance policies but think that there are many benefits to be gained from disclosure.","Try to convince the patient to consider disclosure and offer referral to a genetic counsellor."]

ScenarioTitle: You are talking to the parent of an 8-year-old male patient.
Background: You are talking to the parent of an 8-year-old male patient. The parent is concerned that he is growing a lot faster than his classmates. His older brother had not reached that height by the same age. The boy looks older than 8 years and has a deep voice. His weight, height and measurements confirm that he is in the 90th percentile (i.e., high end of normal) of the standard growth chart.
TasksJson: ["Reassure the parent that being in the 90th percentile range is not necessarily a problem.","Determine how tall the boy\u0027s parents were when they were children.","Discuss the possibility of precocious puberty (high level of hormones that causes growth spurt).","Suggest a referral to a specialist (e.g., paediatric endocrinologist).","Sensitively explain why the referral may be necessary (e.g., child may develop \u0027gigantism\u0027 if his condition is related to excess growth hormone; pituitary adenomas in childhood don\u0027t usually stop unless surgically removed, etc.)."]

ScenarioTitle: You are consulting an 88-year-old who lives independently. You have just given the results from a urine sample.
Background: You are consulting an 88-year-old who lives independently. You have just given the results from a urine sample. The patient has a urinary tract infection (UTI) and has had several proven UTIs recently. The patient is concerned about the recurrence and you are discussing some precautions. His/her general health is good otherwise.
TasksJson: ["Find out about the patient\u0027s diet, fluids, and exercise.","Congratulate the patient on his/her healthy lifestyle. Highlight that good hygiene is also important and educate the patient on \u0027double voiding\u0027 (e.g., emptying bladder, waiting a moment then trying to empty again, etc.).","Suggest treatment with antibiotics (e.g., prescription for trimethoprim 300 mg/day for three days, three month course of low dose nitrofurantoin, etc.).","Reassure the patient that with dedication and patience you expect to be able to resolve the current UTI issues."]

ScenarioTitle: You are speaking to the parent of a five-year-old girl, Linda, who presents with a barking cough, sneeze and fever.
Background: You are speaking to the parent of a five-year-old girl, Linda, who presents with a barking cough, sneeze and fever. Yesterday you diagnosed mild croup and recommended symptom relief and that the parent seeks medical attention should symptoms worsen. The parent has come to see you again today and is very worried that Linda's condition is getting worse.
TasksJson: ["Ask about Linda\u0027s symptoms.","Suggest steroid treatment.","Explain the possible side-effects of the steroid treatment (e.g., suppression of the immune system, predisposition to infection, etc.).","Reassure the patient that steroids are the best treatment for mild croup and give reasons why (e.g., antibiotic will not eliminate viral infection, etc.).","Offer to review Linda\u0027s case in 24 hours."]

ScenarioTitle: You are talking to a parent of a six-year-old boy who has had a sore throat and fever for two days.
Background: You are talking to a parent of a six-year-old boy who has had a sore throat and fever for two days. The parent noticed blood in the boy's urine this morning. The boy looks unwell and has a temperature of 38.5°C. His throat is swollen and red and there is exudate on the tonsils. A full ward test confirms blood in the urine. You diagnose bacterial tonsillitis with kidney involvement (poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis).
TasksJson: ["Explain to the parent the results of the urine test and the diagnosis.","Explain that the child requires further investigation and an urgent appointment with a paediatrician.","Explain that you would like to start a course of antibiotics (penicillin).","Address the parent\u0027s concerns about the use of antibiotics for a \u0027simple\u0027 throat infection by explaining the connection between the infection and the blood in the urine (e.g., the body produces extra antibodies to fight the infection, and these settle in the kidneys causing inflammation, etc.).","Answer the parent\u0027s questions about the next steps in the treatment of his/her son (e.g., refer to a paediatrician to monitor urine and blood pressure and make sure recovery is complete, etc.)."]

ScenarioTitle: Your patient is a 52-year-old smoker. Over the last six months, he/she has experienced occasions of breathlessness and chest pain on exertio
Background: Your patient is a 52-year-old smoker. Over the last six months, he/she has experienced occasions of breathlessness and chest pain on exertion. You diagnose angina after asking about the type of pain.
TasksJson: ["Ask the patient to describe the pain.","Explain your diagnosis: angina (reduced blood/oxygen supply to the heart) and reassure the patient that the condition can be effectively managed.","Explain the need to assess other risk factors \u2013 fasting glucose, cholesterol, BP \u2013 and recommend an immediate assessment by a cardiologist.","Caution against strenuous exercise.","Stress the importance of smoking cessation. Offer to discuss ways of helping the patient to quit smoking."]

ScenarioTitle: Your 52-year-old patient has been admitted to hospital with diverticulitis.
Background: Your 52-year-old patient has been admitted to hospital with diverticulitis. You think it will settle down within one week with some antibiotics. Your patient is a highly anxious person and is concerned that he/she may have bowel cancer because his/her mother died of bowel cancer.
TasksJson: ["Confirm the diagnosis (CT scan) of diverticulitis.","Explain diverticulitis (inflammation of the diverticula, which are outpockets of the bowel mucosa).","Find out about the patient\u0027s family history and explain that family history of bowel cancer is important but prevention and early detection for all people is highly advisable.","Reassure the patient that he/she is doing everything possible to identify any changes that could lead to early detection of cancer (e.g., good diet, awareness of signs and symptoms, regular check-ups, colonoscopy when indicated).","Explain the need to avoid constipation and to maintain a high fibre diet and soft stool consistency."]

ScenarioTitle: This 63-year-old patient is enquiring about the need for a tetanus vaccination.
Background: This 63-year-old patient is enquiring about the need for a tetanus vaccination. He/she cut his/her right foot while working in the garden recently. He/she cleaned the wound but is worried about contracting tetanus.
TasksJson: ["Find out the reasons for the patient\u0027s enquiry.","Check for any symptoms of tetanus \u2018lockjaw\u2019 (e.g., muscle stiffness and spasms in the neck, especially a stiff jaw, 4-21 days after injury).","Explain why tetanus is a serious disease (e.g., affects nervous system, muscles, etc.).","Reassure the patient that the consultation was a good idea (booster required every 10 years: immune system may not work as well with age). Recommend a tetanus vaccination if required (if previous vaccination was more than ten years ago, advise the patient to have another booster).","Encourage the patient\u0027s gardening hobby (outdoor exercise).","Advise on suitable footwear to avoid future gardening injuries (strong, covering the feet, thick soles, etc.)."]

ScenarioTitle: An elderly patient has come to you after an acute episode of diverticulitis.
Background: An elderly patient has come to you after an acute episode of diverticulitis. He/she had acute onset of pain in the left iliac fossa and rectal bleeding for which he/she was hospitalised. The hospital report sent to you indicated no perforation, abscesses, peritonitis or fistula. The patient is extremely anxious as he/she was not given any information about the condition on discharge.
TasksJson: ["Reassure the patient that the hospital report indicates no perforation, etc.","Explain to the patient that the condition could recur.","Stress the importance of dietary modification to avoid constipation. However, excessive use of aperients (purgatives) should be avoided.","Explain why the antibiotic treatment was prescribed (bacterial infection of the colon can cause diverticular disease).","Advise the patient to return if rectal bleeding or bad abdominal pain recurs; a surveillance colonoscopy might be the next step if bowel habit alters or bleeding returns."]

ScenarioTitle: Your patient is 50 years old and has come to enquire about a Boostrix vaccine (combined diphtheria, tetanus and acellular pertussis (dTpa) v
Background: Your patient is 50 years old and has come to enquire about a Boostrix vaccine (combined diphtheria, tetanus and acellular pertussis (dTpa) vaccine). The patient's daughter is going to have a baby and she is encouraging the patient to get the vaccine, as she has heard that some illnesses can be fatal for infants. The patient's daughter believes that if the patient is vaccinated, it will help protect the baby from these illnesses. The patient has come to discuss the matter with you.
TasksJson: ["Ask the patient about his/her reason for presenting today.","Explain what a Boostrix vaccine consists of (e.g., diphtheria, tetanus, whooping cough), and that it is recommended for adults in close contact with newborns.","Persuade the patient to have the injection and give reasons why whooping cough may be fatal to an infant (e.g., severe relentless coughing, hypoxic encephalopathy, may lead to brain damage and even death, etc.).","Explain that the risks of diphtheria and tetanus are low but the vaccine is a three-in-one injection.","Suggest that the patient return next week for the vaccine."]

ScenarioTitle: This 32-year-old patient presents with a three-day history of a painful left ear.
Background: This 32-year-old patient presents with a three-day history of a painful left ear. On examination, there is severe otitis media (inflammation in middle ear) present in the left ear, with a recent small central perforation of the left eardrum and pus visible from the external auditory canal.
TasksJson: ["Explain the diagnosis to the patient.","Explain the mechanism: infection build-up of pus behind eardrum; eventual perforation reduction in pain (pus previously under pressure \u2013 released to flow freely to the outside).","Reassure the patient (e.g., not an unusual occurrence with this condition; small perforation will heal readily; no permanent effect on hearing).","Outline treatment: broad spectrum antibiotic; review at the end of the course, when the perforation can also be reassessed; audiological testing if hearing deficits continue.","Advise against any activities that involve pressure change (e.g., aircraft flight, diving etc) until condition has completely resolved."]

ScenarioTitle: You inform your 42-year-old patient of his/her recent fasting blood glucose test result (7.
Background: You inform your 42-year-old patient of his/her recent fasting blood glucose test result (7.6 mmol/l) which confirms a diagnosis of diabetes mellitus Type II (DM). The test is the patient’s second test this month. The patient challenges your diagnosis.
TasksJson: ["Briefly explain diabetes and its causes (emphasise that you can get \u201Csugar diabetes\u201D even if you don\u2019t eat sugar).","Explain that the thresholds (raised glucose values on two occasions) for diagnosing DM are determined by World Health Organisation (WHO) standards using evidence from research.","Explain that early treatment and regular appointments for monitoring diabetes status (e.g., sugars, blood pressure, cholesterol) will help prevent complications such as blockage of blood vessels to heart, brain and feet, problems with kidney and eyes.","Recommend dietary/lifestyle changes and refer to a dietician/diabetes educator.","Convince the patient to commence preventative measures as the test results are valid and further tests are unnecessary."]

ScenarioTitle: You are speaking to a 40-year-old office worker who fainted on the train yesterday.
Background: You are speaking to a 40-year-old office worker who fainted on the train yesterday. The patient thinks that he/she fainted because the train was hot and crowded but the patient's spouse insisted that he/she come to see you. The patient eats mainly a vegan diet (no dairy or meat). You suspect arrhythmia, which is a common symptom of malnutrition where there may be an electrolyte imbalance.
TasksJson: ["Ask the patient to explain what happened when he/she fainted.","Ask about his/her lifestyle (e.g., diet, work, exercise, etc.).","Ask about other symptoms (e.g., fatigue, irritability, diarrhoea, palpitations, tongue biting, loss of bowel and bladder control, etc.).","Explain your suspected diagnosis (arrhythmia, malnutrition) to the patient.","Persuade the patient to take blood tests to exclude iron deficiency anaemia and to check that other electrolytes are within normal limits.","Encourage the patient to increase protein in his/her diet (e.g., meat, tofu, nuts, etc.) and return for a review in two weeks."]

ScenarioTitle: Your patient has come to see you about his/her 16-year-old son whom he/she suspects is taking illegal drugs.
Background: Your patient has come to see you about his/her 16-year-old son whom he/she suspects is taking illegal drugs. The boy is not present.
TasksJson: ["Ask questions to establish why the parent thinks that his/her son is taking drugs.","Find out more about the boy (his lifestyle, friendship group, studies, etc.).","Find out what your patient would like you to do. Ask whether it would be possible for the boy to come to see you in person.","Suggest referring the boy to an adolescent psychologist for assessment and appropriate treatment.","Explain to the parent some of the possible effects of marijuana (e.g., can affect alertness, concentration, coordination, etc.)."]

ScenarioTitle: Your patient is a 49-year-old accountant, diagnosed six months ago with rheumatoid arthritis (RA).
Background: Your patient is a 49-year-old accountant, diagnosed six months ago with rheumatoid arthritis (RA). The symptoms of joint pain and fatigue have been well-managed with NSAIDs (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs), but one week ago, he/she experienced a ‘flare’ (period when joints are more inflamed and painful). The patient smokes 10 cigarettes per day. He/she is seeking your advice on the anticipated course of the illness and appropriate management.
TasksJson: ["Explain that RA is a chronic disease, which will not just \u2018go away\u2019 (e.g., no cure, remits and relapses, current flare will probably settle but more quickly with medication, etc.).","Provide strategies for coping with RA (e.g., rest, sleep, modify diet, sensible exercise \u2013 long walks, massage, hot treatment, etc.).","Provide reassurance \u2013 early diagnosis and intervention are important for improving patient outcomes.","Advise the patient to stop smoking.","Offer to refer the patient to a rheumatologist for specialist advice and possible cortisone treatment."]

ScenarioTitle: A fifty-year-old patient has come to see you for a routine health check.
Background: A fifty-year-old patient has come to see you for a routine health check. You notice that he/she has gained a lot of weight since last presenting. You discover that his/her BMI is 35 (obese). You know this patient has a family history of heart disease, and that his/her father died suddenly of a heart attack in his fifties.
TasksJson: ["Find out about diet and lifestyle factors; investigate any possible psychological issues.","Convince this patient that he/she must lose weight.","Suggest lifestyle changes the patient can make to facilitate weight loss (e.g., exercise, change diet, etc.). Accept no excuses regarding sedentary work routine or limited mobility.","Impress upon him/her the risks associated with obesity (e.g., cardiovascular disease, diabetes type II etc.).","Suggest a referral to a dietitian, or possibly a psychologist."]

ScenarioTitle: A three-year-old boy has been stung by a bee. Last year, the boy's cousin experienced a severe allergic reaction after being stung by a bee,
Background: A three-year-old boy has been stung by a bee. Last year, the boy's cousin experienced a severe allergic reaction after being stung by a bee, requiring hospitalisation and emergency management. The boy's parent has rushed down to your surgery, as he/she is extremely worried about the risk of developing anaphylaxis (a dangerous allergic reaction). The boy has a large red swelling on his arm and appears to be in a lot of pain.
TasksJson:
["Gently refuse to organise for the child to be admitted to hospital.","Reassure the parent (e.g., localised response; already half an hour after the sting and no signs of systemic illness – hives, wheezing, shortness of breath, faintness or weakness, etc.).","Convince the parent to observe the son at home. Offer the following advice on care at home:
- ice to soothe pain and reduce swelling.
- clean the affected area to avoid infection.
- treat itching with over-the-counter antihistamine (e.g., Benadryl)."]

ScenarioTitle: You are speaking to the son/daughter of your 68-year-old patient, Harry Smith.
Background: You are speaking to the son/daughter of your 68-year-old patient, Harry Smith. Harry has a history of atrial fibrillation (abnormal heart rhythm) and takes warfarin (anticoagulant) to reduce the risk of thrombosis and embolism (abnormal formation and migration of blood clots). The son/daughter is requesting a prescription of Panadeine Forte for Harry, who two days ago fell at home and now has extensive bruising and pain on his right thigh but is otherwise well.
TasksJson: ["Tell the son/daughter that you will not write a prescription for a patient without a consultation.","Explain your decision (standard of care; the importance of patient assessment in management decision; warfarin contraindication).","Express concern about Harry\u2019s well-being and convince the son/daughter that a home visit, with Harry\u2019s consent, is most desirable."]

ScenarioTitle: Your patient describes two syncopal episodes that have occurred in the last three months.
Background: Your patient describes two syncopal episodes that have occurred in the last three months. The patient has come to see you because he/she is worried that it might happen again. The episodes were not witnessed and you do not know if they were truly syncopal, whether they were convulsions, or even if they were real. You want him/her to see a neurologist.
TasksJson: ["Explain that further investigation is necessary for diagnosis, and that you must do an ECG (electrocardiogram) here in the surgery. You also want to do a CT scan of his/her head and some basic blood tests.","Convince the patient that he/she should visit a neurologist, as a cautionary measure. Reassure him/her and explain what tests the neurologist will run, including an electroencephalogram (EEG).","Without alarming him/her, insist that he/she needs to make time to see the neurologist. Persuade the patient not to drive until the situation is clearer (as any car insurance will not cover the patient in the event of an accident until things are sorted out)."]

ScenarioTitle: Your patient is a music journalist and goes to a lot of live rock concerts.
Background: Your patient is a music journalist and goes to a lot of live rock concerts. The patient has been experiencing tinnitus. He/she felt faint yesterday, but did not lose consciousness. The patient seems very concerned about this.
TasksJson: ["Find out about the patient\u0027s history of tinnitus.","Discuss the possible causes of tinnitus (e.g., exposure to loud noise) and symptoms (e.g., loss of equilibrium/balance, etc.). Explain that the tinnitus could have developed without the patient noticing.","Offer to refer the patient to an ENT (ear, nose, throat) specialist and caution the patient against things that could worsen his/her condition (e.g., loud noise can result in hearing loss, etc.).","Warn the patient that tinnitus may be impossible to cure and stress the importance of protecting the ears from loud music.","Persuade the patient to at least try wearing ear plugs."]

ScenarioTitle: An elderly patient has just presented with severe flank pain.
Background: An elderly patient has just presented with severe flank pain. He/she looks pale, and is walking with difficulty due to the pain. You take a urine specimen and discover blood in the urine. You suspect renal calculi (kidney stones).
TasksJson: ["Advise the patient that he/she needs to go to hospital immediately.","Explain the possible diagnosis and why hospital treatment is necessary (e.g., kidney stone may have moved into ureter, etc.).","Explain what is likely to happen in the hospital (e.g., X-ray to find the position of the stone, laser treatment to break up the stone, open surgery very unlikely, etc.).","Reassure the patient, who is terrified of hospitals and resistant to going, by answering his/her questions.","Assure the patient that he/she will not be given penicillin.","Gain permission to call an ambulance for him/her."]

ScenarioTitle: You see the parent of a five-year-old boy who was diagnosed with asthma a couple of days ago, after attending the Emergency Department with
Background: You see the parent of a five-year-old boy who was diagnosed with asthma a couple of days ago, after attending the Emergency Department with a severe bout of coughing, breathing difficulty and wheezing. This is a follow-up appointment. The child is not present for the discussion.
TasksJson: ["Confirm reason for appointment (follow-up following asthma diagnosis). Find out how child has been since hospital visit (severity of asthma, frequency of attacks, effect of treatment, etc.).","Find out further relevant details (any family history of: asthma, eczema, hay fever, etc.). Explore possible triggers of child\u2019s asthma attacks (exposure to: cigarette smoke, dust mites, pollen; exercise; cold air; etc.).","Give information about childhood asthma (chronic lung condition: tightening or narrowing of muscles in airways, swelling/inflammation, production of extra mucus; risk factors: family history of hay fever; etc.). Find out any concerns.","Reassure parent about child\u2019s asthma (e.g., manageable, regular monitoring, support available, etc.). Describe asthma management (e.g., identifying and controlling triggers, assessing severity of symptoms, knowing how to respond in urgent situation, informing child\u2019s school, etc.).","Outline next steps (e.g., examination of child, creation of asthma action plan, discussion of treatment, organising: support, follow-up appointments, etc.). Establish parent\u2019s willingness to bring child into room for examination."]

ScenarioTitle: Your patient is a 40-year-old long-term smoker with a history of epilepsy since childhood.
Background: Your patient is a 40-year-old long-term smoker with a history of epilepsy since childhood. He/she has been trying to quit smoking with no other aids but has been unsuccessful. The patient has come to request that you prescribe him/her Zyban (bupropion), an anti-smoking medication.
TasksJson: ["Enquire about the patient\u0027s smoking history and attempts to quit.","Explain that Zyban is not suitable for epileptics because the drug can cause fits.","Explain that Zyban interferes with the effectiveness of epileptic treatment and that fits can be quite severe (e.g., require hospitalisation, etc.).","Politely refuse to prescribe Zyban and explain that there are other quitting methods available.","Suggest other methods (e.g., nicotine lozenges, patches, etc.) including hypnotherapy (hypnosis to help quit smoking) and recommend that the patient choose a hypnotherapist with a good success rate.","Persuade the patient to return for a review in three weeks."]

ScenarioTitle: Operating Theatre Suite
Background: You are working as a surgical resident in this hospital. You have been called to talk to a 45-year-old patient who is awaiting surgery for a large benign lipoma on his/her back. You note that the patient has already been booked into the outpatient clinic in two weeks for review of the wound and histopathology.
TasksJson: ["Reassure the patient that the risk of cancer is extremely low.", "Explain that the lump will be examined under the microscope and the patient will normally get the results at the two-week review in the clinic. The wound will also be checked then.", "Explain that there will be a scar as it is a large lesion, but it will fade with time. Keeping the area dressed with steristrips for a month can help to minimise this. The surgeon will discuss this further with the patient.", "Reassure the patient about removal of the lump and the unlikelihood of recurrence."]

ScenarioTitle: A 33-year-old patient presents complaining of enlarged cervical and axillary lymph nodes that become worse after drinking alcohol.
Background: A 33-year-old patient presents complaining of enlarged cervical and axillary lymph nodes that become worse after drinking alcohol. The patient has looked on the internet and is convinced it is Hodgkin's lymphoma. He/she is very upset and anxious. On examination, you find no evidence of enlarged spleen or liver, but there is lymphadenopathy in the cervical nodes. You are unable to feel any axillary nodes or supraclavicular nodes.
TasksJson: ["Question the patient about associated symptoms (e.g., fatigue, weight loss, night sweats) and family history.","Reassure the patient that it is unlikely to be serious and explain your findings to him/her (lymphadenopathy in cervical nodes).","Explain what lymphadenopathy is (e.g., swelling of lymph nodes) and what might cause it (e.g., infection, etc.).","Suggest blood tests to investigate possible causes (e.g., complete blood count to show infection, etc.).","Agree to consider referring him/her for specialist opinion after the test results are returned."]

ScenarioTitle: Your 50-year-old patient is an office worker who broke his/her right arm during a fall six weeks ago.
Background: Your 50-year-old patient is an office worker who broke his/her right arm during a fall six weeks ago. The fibreglass cast was due to be removed this week but X-rays reveal that the break is not yet healed. The patient has a medical history of asthma and has been on corticosteroids for three months. You suspect osteoporosis.
TasksJson: ["Ask about the patient\u0027s family history of osteoporosis and other risk factors (e.g., low vitamin D intake, low calcium intake, etc.).","Tell the patient you suspect he/she may have osteoporosis.","Explain osteoporosis (e.g., condition where bones become less dense and more likely to break, etc.).","Refer the patient for bone mineral density testing at the local hospital.","Explain the Dual Energy X-ray Absorptiometry (DEXA) method of bone testing (e.g., X-ray beams of different energy, detects bone and soft tissue separately, safe and painless, usually takes a few minutes, etc.).","Reassure the patient that there are no complications with DEXA testing aside from a small radiation dose."]

ScenarioTitle: Your patient is a 55-year-old aged care assistant. The patient injured his/her right elbow while helping an overweight man out of his chair
Background: Your patient is a 55-year-old aged care assistant. The patient injured his/her right elbow while helping an overweight man out of his chair when the man fell onto him/her. Your patient is returning for the results of the X-ray.
TasksJson: ["Explain that the results show an undisplaced fracture of the olecranon (e.g., tip of the ulna, one of the forearm bones, etc.).","Persuade the patient to take some time off work (e.g., two weeks of full rest followed by a gradual return to work, initially performing alternative duties, etc.).","Sympathise with the patient but stress the need for rest.","Highlight that the treatment will involve pain minimisation and immobilisation (e.g., sling, splint, analgesic, rest, etc.).","Offer to arrange a doctor\u0027s certificate, some analgesics, and a review with an X-ray in two weeks."]

ScenarioTitle: This 35-year-old has recently started having difficulty eating foods that contain milk and milk products.
Background: This 35-year-old has recently started having difficulty eating foods that contain milk and milk products. He/she is experiencing stomach cramps and nausea. You suspect secondary lactose intolerance.
TasksJson: ["Question the patient about his/her symptoms (e.g., flatulence, diarrhoea, etc.).","Find out if the patient has experienced any stomach problems (e.g., gastroenteritis) recently.","Explain your diagnosis - secondary lactose intolerance (e.g., gastroenteritis affects lining of gut, etc.).","Respond to the patient\u0027s argument that he/she cannot be lactose intolerant as there is no history of lactose intolerance in the patient\u0027s family (e.g., secondary lactose intolerance not hereditary, etc.).","Discuss when the condition can be expected to subside (e.g., several weeks as the lining of the gut heals, etc.)."]

ScenarioTitle: The patient, aged 25, presents with tiny, off-white ulcers on the tongue.
Background: The patient, aged 25, presents with tiny, off-white ulcers on the tongue. On examination, the patient clearly has good dental hygiene.
TasksJson: ["Question the patient to exclude diabetes mellitus and inflammatory bowel disease as underlying conditions, and herpes simplex as a cause (fever symptoms?).","You suspect aphthous ulcers (no known cause, but some research suggests an immune reaction - could be related to stress, hormones, virus or allergy).","Recommend a blood test to check for infection.","Discuss management of the symptoms (rinse with warm, salty water or medicated mouthwash, apply antiseptic gel, take paracetamol, have plenty of fluids, avoid spicy and sour foods).","The ulcers will resolve by themselves in a few days.","Offer to prescribe an anti-inflammatory drug if pain persists.","Advise the patient on a healthy lifestyle."]

ScenarioTitle: The parent of a 3-year-old girl is seeking advice and a diagnosis (prior to the receipt of full test results) following the emergency admiss
Setting: Intensive Care Unit at Children's Hospital
Background: The parent of a 3-year-old girl is seeking advice and a diagnosis (prior to the receipt of full test results) following the emergency admission of his/her daughter yesterday. She was suffering from anaphylactic shock, almost certainly as a result of a food allergy. She is currently recovering after the subcutaneous administration of adrenaline. The parent appears calm.
TasksJson:
["Be sympathetic and reassuring.","Include the following information in your response to his/her questions:
- symptoms could have been caused by food/drink at party.
- confirmation of allergen to be done by administration of diagnostic tests.
- explanation of allergy: i.e., immune response (non-toxic substance treated as toxic by immune system), sometimes life-threatening.
- outlook: many children outgrow allergies.
- future prevention: avoid allergen (when identified); inform supervising adults of problem/causes/dangers.
- treatment of possible future episodes: adrenaline (using EpiPen autoinjector), immediate medical attention."]

ScenarioTitle: Your patient is 45 years old, married with three teenage children.
Background: Your patient is 45 years old, married with three teenage children. He/she runs a successful consultancy business. Three months ago, his/her mother-in-law was diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease and is now living with the family. The patient is finding it difficult to balance family and work commitments and is worried about how he/she will manage to support the mother-in-law. Anxiety has been causing your patient to have problems with sleeping at night. He/she has come to see you today to request sleeping pills.
TasksJson: ["Explain to the patient that you are reluctant to prescribe sleeping pills (e.g. risk of dependency, etc.).","Refuse to prescribe sleeping pills but reassure the patient that anxiety can be managed by alternative methods (e.g., self-care techniques, dietary measures, exercise, etc.).","Counsel the patient on the role of stress management and sleep hygiene (e.g., focus on routines and natural rhythms, make sleeping environments more restful, etc.) in relieving anxiety.","Try to convince the patient to accept a referral to see a counsellor/psychologist for stress management."]

ScenarioTitle: You are talking to the parent of an 8-year-old male patient.
Background: You are talking to the parent of an 8-year-old male patient. The parent is concerned that he is growing a lot faster than his classmates. His older brother had not reached that height by the same age. The boy looks older than 8 years and has a deep voice. His weight, height and measurements confirm that he is in the 90th percentile (i.e., high end of normal) of the standard growth chart.
TasksJson: ["Reassure the parent that being in the 90th percentile range is not necessarily a problem.","Determine how tall the boy\u0027s parents were when they were children.","Discuss the possibility of precocious puberty (high level of hormones that causes growth spurt).","Suggest a referral to a specialist (e.g., paediatric endocrinologist).","Sensitively explain why the referral may be necessary (e.g., child may develop \u0027gigantism\u0027 if his condition is related to excess growth hormone; pituitary adenomas in childhood don\u0027t usually stop unless surgically removed, etc.)."]

ScenarioTitle: A parent has brought in his/her nine-year-old daughter who underwent a tonsillectomy a week ago.
Background: A parent has brought in his/her nine-year-old daughter who underwent a tonsillectomy a week ago. The daughter has been using oxycodone quite liberally for post-operative pain, and is now suffering severe constipation. The child has no history of severe constipation and you have already examined the child.
TasksJson: ["Explain the link between the oxycodone and the daughter\u0027s symptoms.","Outline effective measures for resolving the constipation and recommend alternative pain relief.","Discuss whether the parent should avoid giving oxycodone to his/her daughter in the future (e.g., side effects are common but usually mild and short-lived, etc.).","Persuade the parent to be less liberal with the pain medication (e.g., tonsillectomy pain usually improves after first few days, etc.).","Answer questions about the benefits of ice-cream (e.g., eating normally helps the throat to heal, etc.) and salt water gargles (e.g., can relieve a sore throat, important not to swallow, etc.)."]

ScenarioTitle: Your 34-year-old patient, a dancer, has had a Baker's cyst (a popliteal cyst on the back of the knee) for a few months.
Background: Your 34-year-old patient, a dancer, has had a Baker's cyst (a popliteal cyst on the back of the knee) for a few months. At the first presentation you decided to observe it. You are now reviewing the patient who believes the cyst is increasing in size. However, you have measured the cyst and determined that it has not increased.
TasksJson: ["Ask the patient about possible new symptoms (e.g., pain, reduced movement, etc.).","Explain that you want to continue to observe the cyst (e.g., no symptoms or enlargement, etc.). Encourage the patient to continue with the current treatment (i.e., physio, ice, supportive footwear, etc.).","Discuss possible future treatment (e.g., review by a sports physician, orthopaedic surgeon and a knee arthroscopy to evaluate/treat underlying injury or degenerative change, etc.).","Suggest another review in three months."]

ScenarioTitle: An elderly patient presented several months ago with herpes zoster (shingles) on the right temporal region of the face.
Background: An elderly patient presented several months ago with herpes zoster (shingles) on the right temporal region of the face. He/she is now complaining of symptoms of postherpetic neuralgia (the nerve pain that often lingers after a shingles rash goes away).
TasksJson: ["Explain the cause of the symptoms to the patient (pain in the nerves).","Recommend analgesia as a first line of treatment (paracetamol or codeine). Give capsaicin cream for topical application and explain the sensation it might cause. (e.g., a slight stinging sensation or coughing and sneezing, etc.).","Mention anticonvulsant drugs (gabapentin or pregabalin) may be used if necessary.","Answer questions about excision of the affected area and reassure him/her that surgery is not indicated.","Explain that non-pharmacological approaches may help (e.g., relaxation, meditation, psychologist, chronic pain clinic, etc.)."]

ScenarioTitle: Your 41-year-old patient has come for a review appointment. The patient was recently diagnosed with bipolar disorder (a psychiatric conditio
Background: Your 41-year-old patient has come for a review appointment. The patient was recently diagnosed with bipolar disorder (a psychiatric condition characterised by extreme mood changes). He/she has been prescribed sertraline (Zoloft) and his/her condition has stabilised. The patient wishes to discontinue treatment.
TasksJson: ["Discuss how the medication is working.","Ensure the patient has not been experiencing trouble sleeping, suicidal thoughts or other potential side effects.","Explain the importance of continuing to take the medication as prescribed (e.g., stopping medication can cause return of symptoms, etc.).","Try to convince the patient to continue the treatment (e.g., medication appears to be working, etc.).","Reassure the patient, who is anxious that people will think differently of him/her if they find out about his/her bipolar disorder."]

ScenarioTitle: Your patient is a 42-year-old financial adviser. He/she has a stressful job and frequently travels overseas on business.
Background: Your patient is a 42-year-old financial adviser. He/she has a stressful job and frequently travels overseas on business. A few months ago, a work colleague suggested that he/she take sleeping pills to help regulate sleep and ease anxiety. The patient came to see you and you prescribed a benzodiazepine. The patient has now run out of pills and so today he/she has come to request another prescription.
TasksJson: ["Ask the patient how often he/she takes the sleeping pills.","Explain to the patient that long term nightly use of any sleeping pill is not recommended (use of pills does not cure sleep problem; risk of drug dependency).","Tactfully refuse to prescribe another prescription.","Convince the patient to try non-medical interventions - e.g., regular exercise, control workload (learn to say \u2018no\u2019), reduce alcohol/caffeine, etc.","Caution against stopping the pills suddenly (risk of withdrawal symptoms) - gradually decrease the dose and consider other strategies for coping with his/her anxiety."]

ScenarioTitle: Your patient is a 45-year-old office worker who is complaining of fatigue and feeling unwell.
Background: Your patient is a 45-year-old office worker who is complaining of fatigue and feeling unwell. The patient appears to be overweight and thinks he/she may have diabetes. Recent publicity about diabetes (on TV, in the newspaper) has made him/her decide to get a check-up.
TasksJson: ["Find out how patient is feeling (any symptoms, concerns, etc.).","Explore patient\u2019s lifestyle (exercise, work/life balance, etc.).","Discuss possible significance of symptoms (e.g., possible underlying condition such as diabetes, etc.). Reassure patient about his/her symptoms (e.g., different possible causes, diabetes: only one possibility, can be managed, etc.).","Briefly explain diabetes (e.g., type 1: insulin not produced; type 2: insulin not sufficient/effective, etc.). Outline management of diabetes (e.g., medication, diet, exercise, monitoring of blood glucose, etc.).","Outline next steps (diagnostic blood test, return visit for results, consequent assessment of patient\u2019s health and lifestyle, etc.)."]

ScenarioTitle: Your patient is a 50-year-old insurance broker whose recent divorce has been stressful and wants a holiday to restore energy and spirit.
Background: Your patient is a 50-year-old insurance broker whose recent divorce has been stressful and wants a holiday to restore energy and spirit. However, the company boss has refused a request for vacation leave. Your patient has come to see you today to request a medical certificate that will allow him/her to have two weeks off work.
TasksJson: ["Refuse to issue a medical certificate as your patient is not depressed.","Explain that issuing a deliberately false or misleading certificate represents professional misconduct.","Emphasise that misuse of sick leave is a serious matter (e.g., going on vacation while pretending to be sick might have consequences if the boss should question the medical certificate).","Acknowledge that stress affects health and try to convince him/her to see a psychologist for stress management by emphasising the long-term benefits of therapy."]

ScenarioTitle: This 50-year-old patient was recently diagnosed with Parkinson's disease (PD).
Background: This 50-year-old patient was recently diagnosed with Parkinson's disease (PD). You prescribed L-DOPA (levodopa/carbidopa), but the patient is reluctant to continue with it even though he/she is having muscle spasms in the left foot and cannot swing his/her arms. As he/she has no tremors, he/she is keen to try alternative therapies and asks about them instead of taking the prescribed drugs.
TasksJson: ["Encourage him/her to persist with L-DOPA, by explaining the importance of the medication and how it will improve the prognosis.","Explain what PD is (i.e., degenerative disorder of the central nervous system) and what happens neurologically (i.e., often impairs the motor skills, speech and other functions).","Explain that the causes of PD may be due to head trauma, exposure to toxins or simply unknown.","Recommend physiotherapy and explain ways in which it can help (e.g., with movement, initiating gait, pain, breathing, etc).","Answer questions about the benefits of exercise, acupuncture, massage, but emphasise these are not alternatives to the medication."]

ScenarioTitle: This 29-year-old patient ate a whole fish in a restaurant two days ago and thinks that he/she may have a fish bone caught in his/her throat.
Background: This 29-year-old patient ate a whole fish in a restaurant two days ago and thinks that he/she may have a fish bone caught in his/her throat. You have examined the patient's throat and not found any bone, but think that the patient may have scratched his/her oesophagus as it is inflamed and swollen.
TasksJson: ["Ask the patient when the pain started.","Explain that the patient may have a scratched oesophagus.","Assure the patient that the bone is not likely to be caught in his/her throat (e.g., scratch can be as painful, etc.).","Explain the symptoms the patient may experience if a bone is caught in the throat (e.g. vomiting, difficulty swallowing, etc.).","Persuade the patient that the discomfort should go away on its own.","Provide reassurance that if the pain or discomfort doesn\u0027t settle within a few days, an X-ray can be performed, and if needed a referral can be made to a gastroenterologist."]

ScenarioTitle: The parent of a 10-month-old boy has come to see you. The child is suffering from gastroenteritis.
Background: The parent of a 10-month-old boy has come to see you. The child is suffering from gastroenteritis. The parent appears anxious. The child shows no evidence of dehydration. He is passing urine regularly, and is playing happily on the floor of your office.
TasksJson: ["Ask for more details about the child\u2019s symptoms.","Confirm the diagnosis of gastroenteritis and give a brief explanation (i.e., bowel infection, symptoms consistent with parent\u0027s description).","Give advice and reassurance to the parent.","Explain the inappropriateness of any medication other than Gastrolyte (or equivalent), a saline glucose solution.","Advise the parent on suitable food intake (e.g., continue breastfeeding more frequently, child may refuse food initially, etc.)."]

ScenarioTitle: Your 34-year-old patient, a dancer, has had a Baker's cyst (a popliteal cyst on the back of the knee) for a few months.
Background: Your 34-year-old patient, a dancer, has had a Baker's cyst (a popliteal cyst on the back of the knee) for a few months. At the first presentation you decided to observe it. You are now reviewing the patient who believes the cyst is increasing in size. However, you have measured the cyst and determined that it has not increased.
TasksJson: ["Ask the patient about possible new symptoms (e.g., pain, reduced movement, etc.).","Explain that you want to continue to observe the cyst (e.g., no symptoms or enlargement, etc.). Encourage the patient to continue with the current treatment (i.e., physio, ice, supportive footwear, etc.).","Discuss possible future treatment (e.g., review by a sports physician, orthopaedic surgeon and a knee arthroscopy to evaluate/treat underlying injury or degenerative change, etc.).","Suggest another review in three months."]

ScenarioTitle: A parent comes in to ask about his/her eight-year-old daughter because he/she has noticed an unusual symptom.
Background: A parent comes in to ask about his/her eight-year-old daughter because he/she has noticed an unusual symptom. Although the child seems well, blood has started appearing in her urine. The parent is concerned, and becomes increasingly anxious as the consultation progresses.
TasksJson:
["Ask the parent about his/her daughter's recent symptoms and general health.","Respond to the parent's concerns. Include the following information:
- Blood in the urine is not a usual symptom for a young child.
- It may not be serious, but is worth investigating.
- It is too soon to say what this symptom might indicate.
- The child will have to have a blood test initially, to be performed immediately.
- The results of the blood test will be available in 24 hours, and the patient should book another appointment as soon as possible to discuss them.
- This symptom could indicate some problem with the child's kidney function.","Be sympathetic and reassuring."]

ScenarioTitle: An elderly patient has just presented with severe flank pain.
Background: An elderly patient has just presented with severe flank pain. He/she looks pale, and is walking with difficulty due to the pain. You take a urine specimen and discover blood in the urine. You suspect renal calculi (kidney stones).
TasksJson: ["Advise the patient that he/she needs to go to hospital immediately.","Explain the possible diagnosis and why hospital treatment is necessary (e.g., kidney stone may have moved into ureter, etc.).","Explain what is likely to happen in the hospital (e.g., X-ray to find the position of the stone, laser treatment to break up the stone, open surgery very unlikely, etc.).","Reassure the patient, who is terrified of hospitals and resistant to going, by answering his/her questions.","Assure the patient that he/she will not be given penicillin.","Gain permission to call an ambulance for him/her."]

ScenarioTitle: A 47-year-old presents with an attack of gout (intense pain, swelling and inflammation in the joint of his/her right big toe).
Background: A 47-year-old presents with an attack of gout (intense pain, swelling and inflammation in the joint of his/her right big toe). The attack seems much worse than two previous attacks. This time, the patient has taken aspirin for the pain but the pain is getting worse. The patient is seeking your advice on how to relieve the pain. He/she has little knowledge about gout.
TasksJson: ["Explain gout to the patient (build up of uric acid leading to crystalising).","Advise on appropriate pain relief (avoid aspirin) and medical preventive treatment (allopurinol).","Tell the patient that it might take several weeks to get better.","Reassure the patient that recurrent attacks are common but can be prevented.","Educate the patient on how to reduce the frequency of attacks (e.g., modify diet, reduce alcohol consumption, lose weight, etc.)."]

ScenarioTitle: This 29-year-old patient ate a whole fish in a restaurant two days ago and thinks that he/she may have a fish bone caught in his/her throat.
Background: This 29-year-old patient ate a whole fish in a restaurant two days ago and thinks that he/she may have a fish bone caught in his/her throat. You have examined the patient's throat and not found any bone, but think that the patient may have scratched his/her oesophagus as it is inflamed and swollen.
TasksJson: ["Ask the patient when the pain started.","Explain that the patient may have a scratched oesophagus.","Assure the patient that the bone is not likely to be caught in his/her throat (e.g., scratch can be as painful, etc.).","Explain the symptoms the patient may experience if a bone is caught in the throat (e.g. vomiting, difficulty swallowing, etc.).","Persuade the patient that the discomfort should go away on its own.","Provide reassurance that if the pain or discomfort doesn\u0027t settle within a few days, an X-ray can be performed, and if needed a referral can be made to a gastroenterologist."]

ScenarioTitle: Your patient is a 49-year-old accountant, married with two children.
Background: Your patient is a 49-year-old accountant, married with two children. He/she presented three weeks ago with a one-month history of rectal bleeding, diarrhoea and 2kg weight loss. You requested a colonoscopy and today the patient is returning for the results. Unfortunately, the patient has a tumour in the descending colon and the biopsy result confirms cancer.
TasksJson: ["Tell the patient the biopsy results (2cm tumour, confined to bowel wall) and recommend urgent referral to a surgeon.","Explain that management of the illness after surgery may include chemo/radiotherapy, depending on the spread of the tumour (but only with patient\u0027s consent).","Explain that a colostomy is unlikely as the tumour is confined to descending colon.","Encourage the patient to be optimistic about surgery (e.g., success rates are usually high; biopsy indicates that tumour is limited to bowel wall)."]

ScenarioTitle: The patient is a five-year-old girl. She and her family are in Australia visiting friends.
Background: The patient is a five-year-old girl. She and her family are in Australia visiting friends. She has a small, superficial dog bite wound on the side of the face, near the hair line. You are speaking to her parent.
TasksJson: ["Calm the parent.
