Outline what to avoid during recovery (e.g., heavy lifting, bending over, strenuous exercise, dusty/smoky/crowded places, etc.).","Explain patient is to be given discharge pack (e.g., details of follow-up appointment, aftercare instructions, helpline phone numbers, etc.). Check patient is being collected."]

ScenarioTitle: Your patient is 78 years old and was discharged a week ago following a coronary artery bypass graft (CABG).
Background: Your patient is 78 years old and was discharged a week ago following a coronary artery bypass graft (CABG). You visit him/her to check on his/her progress. You have just completed clinical observations. You suspect dehydration.
TasksJson: ["Give findings of your clinical observations (normal: temperature, pulse, respiration, oxygen saturation; no cause for concern; etc.). Find out how patient has been since your last visit (improvement in energy/appetite, reduction in wound pain, any other symptoms, etc.).","Find out more details about symptoms (onset, duration of dizzy spells, amount/appearance of urine, etc.).","Find out about fluid intake (type, quantity, frequency, etc.).","Give possible reason for symptoms (dehydration: caused by low fluid intake, etc.). Advise need for urgent doctor appointment (e.g., confirmation of diagnosis, ruling out other causes related to recent surgery, etc.). Find out reason for patient\u0027s limited fluid intake.","Stress importance of good hydration (e.g., avoiding dizziness, aiding healthy bodily functions/recovery, etc.). Make recommendations (e.g., increasing fluid intake, keeping drink close by, recording daily number of drinks, etc.). Offer to make doctor appointment for patient."]

ScenarioTitle: Your patient is 35 years old and spilled a hot drink on his/her legs and feet, resulting in painful scalding.
Background: Your patient is 35 years old and spilled a hot drink on his/her legs and feet, resulting in painful scalding. You see him/her in triage to establish the details of the accident and to explain the next steps.
TasksJson: ["Find out reason for patient\u0027s visit to Emergency Department.","Find out more details about the drink spill (how long ago, through clothing/on bare skin, hot/boiling drink, action taken, etc.).","Confirm patient\u0027s actions appropriate (e.g., stopping/slowing scalding process, cooling skin, reducing/controlling pain, etc.). Find out if any pain relief taken, etc.).","Explain next steps (e.g., assessment by nurse, administration of pain relief, examination by doctor, treatment, etc.).","Explain hospital admission unlikely to be necessary (e.g., discharge following treatment/prescription medication, etc.).","Resist request to comment on scarring (discussion with doctor after assessment/treatment, etc.). Make recommendations (e.g., take pain relief, wait for examination, etc.). Establish patient\u0027s consent for examination."]

ScenarioTitle: A young boy aged 4, was admitted to hospital through the Children's Emergency Department for acute meningoencephalitis as a result of a comp
Background: A young boy aged 4, was admitted to hospital through the Children's Emergency Department for acute meningoencephalitis as a result of a complication following mumps. He has fully recovered and is ready to be discharged home. His parents are unaware that a vaccine is available in Australia which protects against mumps. They would like further information and guidance regarding vaccination for Mumps. They also have a 2 year old son and have only lived in Australia 6 months.
TasksJson: ["Explain to the parent that the boy has fully recovered.","Make him/her aware of the importance of a full vaccination program for both children.","Tell them what vaccination is required for mumps and when to have it.","Inform about the risks and benefits of the vaccination for mumps.","Explain any side effects that might occur from the vaccination.","Tell them that vaccination is a requirement of many schools.","Tell them that vaccinations can be obtained from free health clinics."]

ScenarioTitle: You are speaking to an 18-year-old boy/girl who had presented to the clinic yesterday complaining of generalized weakness, lethargy, and ina
Background: You are speaking to an 18-year-old boy/girl who had presented to the clinic yesterday complaining of generalized weakness, lethargy, and inability to do the routine work from previous few weeks. He/She also complained of breathlessness while climbing stairs for his/her house. Upon examination, the doctor advised a blood test which revealed that his/her Hemoglobin was 8 g/dl. The normal range of Hemoglobin is between 11-16 g/dl. Given the findings of his/her physical examination, the doctor suspects that the patient is anemic and has asked you to speak to him/her. The patient does not know her test results yet.
TasksJson: ["Explain that his/her HB is low due to which he/she is suffering from anemia","Reassure him/her that anemia is a common condition and is easily treatable","Briefly, explain about anemia (not enough Hemoglobin/red blood cells in the blood)","Outline some treatment options increase iron intake in diet with foods like red meat/steak, leafy green vegetables like spinach/kale, iron fortified cereals, meet dietician for dietary advice, a course of iron tablets- need to be taken after meal to avoid side effects)","Offer a patient information leaflet about anemia","Ask him/her to come back in 4 weeks\u0027 time for another blood test"]

ScenarioTitle: A general practitioner has asked you to visit a patient who has diabetes.
Background: A general practitioner has asked you to visit a patient who has diabetes. Until recently the diabetes has been moderately well controlled by diet and oral medication. However, recently the patient’s blood sugars have been high and the doctor has decided to commence insulin injections. The doctor wants you to show the patient how to give himself/herself the insulin injections.
TasksJson: ["Find out how the patient feels about insulin injections.","Explain slowly and clearly the whole process of giving the injection (including using clean needles, administering the injection, sites for injection etc.).","Try to reassure the patient that he/she will be able to manage the injections.","Emphasise the importance of safe needle disposal (suitable containers, proper care and handling)."]

ScenarioTitle: Discharge advice after laparoscopic appendectomy
Background: You are the staff nurse on a surgical day-ward. Your patient had a laparoscopic appendectomy this morning, is awake, eating sips of water, and is now medically cleared for discharge. The patient lives alone and works as a long-haul truck driver. The discharge pack includes simple analgesia, a wound review appointment in 7 days, and written instructions.
TasksJson: ["Find out how the patient is feeling now and check pain levels.", "Explain the discharge medication plan in plain language, including when and how often to take each medicine.", "Cover wound care: keeping dressings dry, what to look for, and when to seek urgent help.", "Address the patient's concerns about returning to driving and work.", "Confirm understanding and arrange follow-up."]

ScenarioTitle: Medication review with an older adult on polypharmacy
Background: You are the community nurse visiting Mrs Park at home for a routine medication review. She lives alone, takes eight regular medicines for hypertension, heart failure, type 2 diabetes, and osteoarthritis. The pharmacy's last refill record shows she is collecting only half the expected amount of her diuretic. Her last BP reading at the GP surgery was elevated.
TasksJson: ["Open a conversation about how she manages her tablets each day.", "Sensitively explore whether she is taking all her medicines as prescribed.", "Explain in plain language why the 'water tablet' matters for her heart and breathing.", "Agree a practical plan that improves adherence without overwhelming her.", "Plan a brief follow-up check."]

ScenarioTitle: Home wound-care teaching for a venous leg ulcer
Background: You are the practice nurse. Mr Vargas attends for his fortnightly leg-ulcer review. The ulcer is granulating well under compression bandaging. He wants to learn how to manage simple dressing changes at home between clinic visits so he can return to gardening. The wound is currently clean with no signs of infection.
TasksJson: ["Acknowledge his progress and ask about any concerns since the last visit.", "Demonstrate or explain the basic dressing-change technique in a way he can repeat at home.", "Outline signs of wound infection that should prompt a phone call to the clinic.", "Discuss compression hosiery care and skin hydration between dressings.", "Check understanding and arrange the next review."]

ScenarioTitle: Falls-risk discussion with a worried daughter
PatientName: Mrs Joan Whitford (patient, not in room)
Background: Mrs Whitford was admitted three days ago after a fall at home. She has made a good recovery and is medically ready for discharge tomorrow. Her daughter has asked to speak with you privately. The team has flagged Mrs Whitford as a moderate falls risk; a community falls-prevention referral has been arranged.
TasksJson: ["Welcome the daughter and find out what is most concerning her.", "Explain the falls-risk assessment findings in plain language.", "Outline the discharge plan and the community supports being arranged.", "Address the daughter's request that her mother not be sent home.", "Agree practical next steps and offer a contact point."]

ScenarioTitle: Childhood vaccination conversation with a hesitant parent
PatientName: Lily (8 months, daughter of the parent)
Background: You are the practice nurse running the routine 8-month immunisation clinic. Lily is otherwise well. Her mother attended for the appointment but is asking detailed questions about the vaccines, having read concerning posts in an online parenting group. No vaccines have been refused before today; the mother does want to do the right thing.
TasksJson: ["Welcome the parent and explore what specifically is worrying her.", "Listen without dismissing her concerns and acknowledge her motivation.", "Explain the benefits of today's vaccines and the most common short-term reactions in plain language.", "Address the specific worry she raises without overloading her with statistics.", "Agree a next step that respects her right to decide."]

ScenarioTitle: You are discussing discharge planning with a 71-year-old patient following surgery and rehabilitation for a fractured hip.
Background: You are discussing discharge planning with a 71-year-old patient following surgery and rehabilitation for a fractured hip. The patient lives alone and wants to remain independent.
TasksJson: ["Explore the patient\u0027s main concerns about returning home and their previous level of independence.","Find out relevant details about the home environment, stairs, bathroom arrangements, daily activities and available support.","Acknowledge the patient\u0027s wish to remain independent while explaining why temporary support may improve safety.","Discuss possible equipment or home adaptations and practical strategies for bathing, dressing and mobility.","Agree on next steps in discharge planning, including any home assessment or follow-up, and check for remaining concerns."]

ScenarioTitle: You have just completed a functional assessment with a 55-year-old patient recovering from a stroke, focusing on dressing and preparing a si
Background: You have just completed a functional assessment with a 55-year-old patient recovering from a stroke, focusing on dressing and preparing a simple drink.
TasksJson: ["Thank the patient for completing the assessment and explain the main functional findings in respectful, non-technical language.","Acknowledge the patient\u0027s embarrassment and frustration and identify which parts of the tasks were most difficult.","Explain the purpose of compensatory techniques and how they can support independence while recovery and rehabilitation continue.","Link practice of everyday tasks to the patient\u0027s longer-term goal of returning to work.","Agree on priority goals and exercises/activities for the next stage. Check understanding and motivation."]

ScenarioTitle: You see a 42-year-old office worker for an initial occupational therapy assessment because persistent wrist pain is affecting work, cooking
Background: You see a 42-year-old office worker for an initial occupational therapy assessment because persistent wrist pain is affecting work, cooking and childcare.
TasksJson: ["Find out which tasks provoke symptoms, how the patient currently manages them, and the impact on work, home and childcare roles.","Explore the patient\u0027s concerns about damage and any avoidance of normal activity.","Explain the principle of balancing protection, pacing and gradual activity rather than complete rest unless medically indicated.","Discuss practical ergonomic changes, task modification and appropriate splint use if relevant.","Agree on functional goals and a review plan. Check the patient\u0027s understanding and confidence."]

ScenarioTitle: You are reviewing a 68-year-old patient at home after a fall.
Background: You are reviewing a 68-year-old patient at home after a fall. At the previous visit, you recommended environmental changes and bathroom equipment, but adherence has been partial.
TasksJson: ["Review any new falls or near-falls and ask how the patient has managed since the last visit.","Explore the reasons for not following all recommendations, including comfort, identity and concerns about dependence.","Explain the risk factors in a non-judgmental way and relate them to the patient\u0027s goal of staying safely at home.","Negotiate realistic alternatives where possible rather than insisting on every recommendation in one way.","Agree on a revised fall-prevention plan and specific changes to trial before the next review."]

ScenarioTitle: You are speaking with a wheelchair user whose replacement chair has been delayed.
Background: You are speaking with a wheelchair user whose replacement chair has been delayed. The patient is angry, reports increasing discomfort in the current chair, and feels communication from the service has been poor.
TasksJson: ["Acknowledge the patient\u0027s frustration and apologise for the communication problem without becoming defensive.","Clarify the current discomfort, sitting tolerance and any skin changes that may require urgent review.","Explain what is known about the delay and avoid promising a delivery date unless it is confirmed.","Offer appropriate interim measures such as seating review, pressure-relief strategies or temporary equipment if available.","Agree on exactly how and when the patient will be updated. Check that the immediate safety plan is acceptable."]

ScenarioTitle: You are reviewing a 29-year-old contact-lens wearer with increasing dryness and irritation.
Background: You are reviewing a 29-year-old contact-lens wearer with increasing dryness and irritation. The patient reports very long daily wear, occasional sleeping in lenses and frequent use of redness-relief drops.
TasksJson: ["Clarify the symptoms, lens-wearing schedule, hygiene, sleeping in lenses, replacement frequency and any pain, discharge or visual change.","Explain how excessive wear and sleeping in lenses can increase irritation and risk, and why symptoms should not simply be masked with redness-relief drops.","Discuss safer wearing time, lens-free periods, appropriate lubrication if suitable and correct cleaning/replacement practices.","Explain when contact lenses should be stopped immediately and urgent review sought.","Discuss whether refitting or a different lens type may be considered after the eye surface is reassessed. Agree on a plan."]

ScenarioTitle: You have just examined a 47-year-old patient with increasing near-vision difficulty.
Background: You have just examined a 47-year-old patient with increasing near-vision difficulty. Distance vision and ocular health are satisfactory, and the findings are consistent with age-related loss of near focusing ability.
TasksJson: ["Thank the patient for completing the examination and explain the findings in clear, non-technical language.","Explain age-related change in near focusing and reassure the patient that this does not mean the eyes are becoming damaged or weak.","Address the misconception that reading glasses make the eyes dependent or worsen vision.","Discuss suitable options for near correction based on the patient\u0027s needs and daily activities.","Answer questions about exercises or avoiding glasses, and check the patient\u0027s understanding and preference."]

ScenarioTitle: You are reviewing a patient one week after collection of new spectacles.
Background: You are reviewing a patient one week after collection of new spectacles. The patient is angry because of headaches and an unusual spatial sensation, although distance vision is clear.
TasksJson: ["Acknowledge the patient\u0027s frustration and the cost/expectation involved. Avoid dismissing the symptoms as merely needing time.","Clarify exactly what the patient experiences, when symptoms occur and how long the spectacles have been worn.","Check relevant factors such as prescription, fitting/centration, lens design and whether the glasses match the order before assuming adaptation.","Explain that some prescriptions or lens designs can require adaptation, but confirm that the spectacles will be checked and corrected if there is a problem.","Agree on a practical plan for wear, review or remake as appropriate, and confirm how the patient will be followed up."]

ScenarioTitle: You see a 41-year-old contact-lens wearer with acute unilateral red eye, pain, photophobia and reduced vision after sleeping in contact lens
Background: You see a 41-year-old contact-lens wearer with acute unilateral red eye, pain, photophobia and reduced vision after sleeping in contact lenses. The presentation requires urgent same-day medical assessment.
TasksJson: ["Clarify the onset, severity, vision change, discharge, contact-lens wear and any previous treatment.","Acknowledge the patient\u0027s wish for a quick solution but explain that pain, photophobia and reduced vision in a contact-lens wearer are concerning features.","Advise the patient to remove and not reinsert contact lenses and not to use old medication without assessment.","Explain the need for urgent same-day ophthalmic/medical review and what the referral process will involve.","Check that the patient understands the urgency and agrees not to drive if vision is significantly affected."]

ScenarioTitle: You see a 35-year-old graphic designer reporting eye fatigue, dryness and intermittent blurred vision after prolonged screen use.
Background: You see a 35-year-old graphic designer reporting eye fatigue, dryness and intermittent blurred vision after prolonged screen use.
TasksJson: ["Find out more about the symptoms, timing, screen-working habits, breaks, environment and current spectacle/contact-lens use.","Explore relevant eye history and any red-flag symptoms such as persistent pain, marked redness or sudden visual change.","Explain likely contributors to digital eye strain and dryness in clear language.","Address the patient\u0027s concern that normal screen use is permanently damaging the eyes and explain why stronger glasses bought without assessment may not solve the problem.","Give practical management advice and explain when review or further assessment would be appropriate."]

ScenarioTitle: This client has come in to the pharmacy with a cut on the leg that he/she sustained a few days ago, when he/she scraped against some coral w
Background: This client has come in to the pharmacy with a cut on the leg that he/she sustained a few days ago, when he/she scraped against some coral while diving. The client wants a topical application to heal it. On examination, you notice that it is ulcerated, with a septic sloughing base. You insist that the patient needs to see a doctor immediately. However, he/she is reluctant to do so.

ScenarioTitle: Your client has a 5-year-old son who recently commenced antibiotics for a chest infection.
Background: Your client has a 5-year-old son who recently commenced antibiotics for a chest infection. A rash has appeared on his right arm (two ring-shaped lesions, one the size of a coin, the other 5cm diameter). You recognise the rash as ringworm but your client is worried the rash is due to an allergic reaction to antibiotics.
TasksJson: ["Explain that the diagnosis is not a reaction to antibiotics but ringworm.","Answer the client\u0027s question about whether or not to stop giving antibiotics to his/her son.","Give information about ringworm (e.g., a fungal infection; will resolve in 2-4 weeks; use topical ointment; take care of personal hygiene, etc.).","Reassure the client that there are no signs of a serious allergic reaction (e.g., difficulty breathing, dizziness, swollen throat/tongue, etc.).","Explain that it is important to complete the course of antibiotics and advise him/her to consult the doctor if the rash persists after two weeks of treatment."]

ScenarioTitle: Your client has a flu and is complaining of a sore throat, blocked nose and headache.
Background: Your client has a flu and is complaining of a sore throat, blocked nose and headache. The client has a fever of 38°C, and is feeling hot and cold. He/she has aching muscles, joints and has a cough.
TasksJson: ["Explain that rest and plenty of fluids are essential. You understand that work is important, but make it clear that feeling so unwell and work involving driving can be dangerous.","Explain that the flu virus will get worse before it gets better as the body\u0027s immune system fights the virus. White or slightly yellow mucus may develop or if symptoms worsen, yellow or green mucus may develop.","Suggest bed rest, fluids and paracetamol. Lozenges are a good idea and nasal spray may be used for a few days to avoid rebound congestion.","Emphasise there are no quick remedies and rest is best advisable. If symptoms persist go to the doctor."]

ScenarioTitle: A client visits the pharmacy wanting advice on treatment for head lice.
Background: A client visits the pharmacy wanting advice on treatment for head lice. He/she has a child at home suffering with itchy scalp, and when the hair was checked, eggs and lice were found in the child's hair. He/she wants you to recommend treatment for the condition.
TasksJson: ["Ask the client to explain the child\u0027s condition.","Reassure the client that head lice in children attending kindergarten and school is quite common.","Explain that you have a number of treatments on the shelf and that he/she should read and follow the directions carefully.","Explain the wet combing method using conditioner (requires a lot of patience) if non-insecticide based product is insisted upon.","Explain ways to prevent re-infestation (e.g., tying hair back, avoiding sharing hair brushes, checking head weekly, etc.).","Explain the importance of the client washing the bed linen in 60 degree water or dry in dryer on hot cycle for 20 minutes."]

ScenarioTitle: A 58-year-old patient, who is three weeks post-heart attack, was prescribed bisoprolol upon discharge.
Background: A 58-year-old patient, who is three weeks post-heart attack, was prescribed bisoprolol upon discharge. He/she is now concerned about the side effects of this medication.
TasksJson: ["Find out reason for client\u0027s visit.","Outline most common side effects of bisoprolol (e.g., bradycardia, low mood, fatigue, dyspnoea, etc.). Find out how he/she is managing his/her medication (compliance, etc.).","Explore his/her reasons for wanting a lower dose (e.g., side effects, information received, etc.). Explain dose depends on individual client (e.g., recovery rate, doctor\u0027s assessment etc.).","Reassure client fatigue is normal post-heart attack (e.g., to improve with time, etc.). Stress importance of continuing medication at current dose (e.g., reduction in risk of future heart attacks, following doctor\u0027s prescription/advice etc.).","Emphasise inability to dispense lower dose without prescription (e.g., risk to client\u0027s safety, pharmacists must follow protocol, etc.). Suggest appointment with his/her doctor (e.g., discussion of specific problems, adapting dose etc.)."]

ScenarioTitle: The client has come to collect a script for tramadol, a strong pain-relieving tablet.
Background: The client has come to collect a script for tramadol, a strong pain-relieving tablet. He/she also asks for a bottle of St John's wort (Hypericum perforatum), a herbal preparation that may help with depression. The client has been taking the tramadol regularly for severe back pain; he/she has been experiencing a low mood for some time.
TasksJson: ["Find out why the client wants to buy St John\u0027s wort, and what he/she knows about it.","Explain that it would be dangerous to mix the herbal treatment with strong pain-relieving medication. There is an interaction between tramadol and St John\u0027s wort that could lead to a serious reaction (e.g., tremors, seizures, possible death, etc.).","Answer any questions, and make sure that the client understands why you strongly advise against buying the herbal antidepressant.","Persuade the client to visit his/her doctor to discuss the low moods and possible treatment options, including non-drug treatments."]

ScenarioTitle: Your patient is complaining of a red, itchy, watery eye that feels like it has grit in it.
Background: Your patient is complaining of a red, itchy, watery eye that feels like it has grit in it. He/she does not have discharge from the eye. You diagnose Red Eye.
TasksJson: ["Explain he/she has a condition called Red Eye. It can be caused by an infection, an irritation or an allergy.","Suggest using Albalon A (naphazoline) that has an antihistamine and a decongestant (eye drops).","Reassure the patient that the eye has no discharge and the treatment should clear the eye irritation before the wedding.","Explain that the eye drops should not be used for more than one week and if the condition has not improved, the patient may need to get an anti-allergy eye drop or consult a doctor.","Find out if the patient has a heart condition.","Explain that the medication should not be used by a patient with a heart condition."]

ScenarioTitle: Your client is a 42-year-old retail marketing manager who has a five-year history of mild irritable bowel syndrome (IBS).
Background: Your client is a 42-year-old retail marketing manager who has a five-year history of mild irritable bowel syndrome (IBS). In the last month, the client has experienced symptoms of diarrhoea, abdominal bloating and nausea, which are more severe than usual. The client has recently moved house and commenced a new job. He/she requests medication to relieve the nausea and diarrhoea. The client is worried about the condition becoming worse and seeks your advice on the management of IBS.
TasksJson: ["Reassure the client that the condition can be managed (e.g., De-Gas or peppermint oil: relief of bloating; loperamide: antidiarrhoeal, etc.).","Explain that stress factors (e.g., moving house, new job, etc.) may exacerbate IBS.","Stress the importance of diet and lifestyle in minimising symptoms (e.g., low-fat, low-sugar, high-fibre diet) and for long-term management (e.g., loperamide can only be used short-term).","Encourage the client to see a doctor if symptoms persist."]

ScenarioTitle: This client has come to the pharmacy with a prescription for dicloxacillin (a penicillin antibiotic) to treat a skin infection on his/her ri
Background: This client has come to the pharmacy with a prescription for dicloxacillin (a penicillin antibiotic) to treat a skin infection on his/her right leg. Whilst discussing the medication, you discover that the client is allergic to penicillins. Last time this client had amoxicillin (another penicillin antibiotic), he/she experienced an itchy rash all over the body. You think the prescribing doctor is probably unaware of the allergy, and that the client should go back to discuss it.
TasksJson: ["Ask the client about his/her previous allergic reactions to medication, including penicillin.","Ask if the client has recently changed doctors. If so, has the new doctor been told about the previous allergic reaction to penicillin?","Explain that dicloxacillin and amoxicillin are both penicillins, and it is therefore highly likely that the client will be allergic to both.","Be tactful, but persuade the client to return to the doctor for another consultation. Explain that there are other suitable antibiotics such as cefalexin which could be used to treat this skin infection."]

ScenarioTitle: Your client has a flu and is complaining of a sore throat, blocked nose and headache.
Background: Your client has a flu and is complaining of a sore throat, blocked nose and headache. The client has a fever of 38°C, and is feeling hot and cold. He/she has aching muscles, joints and has a cough.
TasksJson: ["Explain that rest and plenty of fluids are essential. You understand that work is important, but make it clear that feeling so unwell and work involving driving can be dangerous.","Explain that the flu virus will get worse before it gets better as the body\u0027s immune system fights the virus. White or slightly yellow mucus may develop or if symptoms worsen, yellow or green mucus may develop.","Suggest bed rest, fluids and paracetamol. Lozenges are a good idea and nasal spray may be used for a few days to avoid rebound congestion.","Emphasise there are no quick remedies and rest is best advisable. If symptoms persist go to the doctor."]

ScenarioTitle: A client visits the pharmacy wanting advice on treatment for head lice.
Background: A client visits the pharmacy wanting advice on treatment for head lice. He/she has a child at home suffering with itchy scalp, and when the hair was checked, eggs and lice were found in the child's hair. He/she wants you to recommend treatment for the condition.
TasksJson: ["Ask the client to explain the child\u0027s condition.","Reassure the client that head lice in children attending kindergarten and school is quite common.","Explain that you have a number of treatments on the shelf and that he/she should read and follow the directions carefully.","Explain the wet combing method using conditioner (requires a lot of patience) if non-insecticide based product is insisted upon.","Explain ways to prevent re-infestation (e.g., tying hair back, avoiding sharing hair brushes, checking head weekly, etc.).","Explain the importance of the client washing the bed linen in 60 degree water or dry in dryer on hot cycle for 20 minutes."]

ScenarioTitle: This 42-year-old reports a mild, but annoying headache which started today.
Background: This 42-year-old reports a mild, but annoying headache which started today. In the past 24 hours, he/she has stopped consuming tea, coffee, cola and chocolate, after reading that caffeine is bad for health. He/she seems anxious.
TasksJson: ["Explain that headaches are a common consequence of stopping drinking tea or coffee (i.e., caffeine withdrawal).","Recommend possible courses of action (e.g., taking over-the-counter painkillers to reduce headache symptoms, reducing the amount of caffeine gradually, maintaining overall fluid intake, waiting for the symptoms to pass in 2-3 days, etc.).","Reassure the client that a more serious cause is unlikely. Explain when to see a doctor (e.g., if the headache persists for more than 24 hours after starting painkillers; problems with balance; visual disturbances; memory loss; fever; joint or muscle pain, etc.)."]

ScenarioTitle: This 34-year-old client thinks he/she may have a peptic ulcer and has come to your pharmacy to request Prilosec (omeprazole), an over-the-co
Background: This 34-year-old client thinks he/she may have a peptic ulcer and has come to your pharmacy to request Prilosec (omeprazole), an over-the-counter proton pump inhibitor. You need to establish whether this medication would be suitable for the client.
TasksJson: ["Ask about the client\u0027s history with this medication, diagnosis and symptoms.","Explain that the client\u0027s condition is more likely to be gastric reflux.","Give the client information about the condition (e.g., more common than peptic ulcer, results from acid stomach contents rising upwards from stomach, etc.).","Ensure the client is not experiencing blood in vomit or bowel motions or taking any blood thinning medications (e.g., aspirin, etc.).","Recommend antacid medication and encourage the client to see a doctor if the medicine does not relieve the symptoms, or if the episodes become more frequent (e.g., may require further investigation and/or prescription medication, etc.)."]

ScenarioTitle: A regular client comes into the pharmacy complaining that his/her heartburn (a chronic problem) appears to be getting worse, and that he/she
Background: A regular client comes into the pharmacy complaining that his/her heartburn (a chronic problem) appears to be getting worse, and that he/she is experiencing extreme indigestive discomfort. The patient hates seeing doctors, and wants you to provide something for the discomfort. You have concerns that the symptoms may be due to more serious problems.
TasksJson: ["Ask about recent symptoms. Explain that sometimes other problems can mimic indigestion \u2014 tactfully give examples (e.g., heart rhythm disturbances, heart failure, heart attack, side effects from medication, etc.).","Outline the tests a doctor might recommend to diagnose the cause (e.g., a stress test for the heart, breath test for H. pylori stomach ulceration, endoscopy, etc.).","When the patient asks for medication, point out that none of the usual non-prescription medications for indigestion are likely to help and explain how they could be dangerous in an undiagnosed situation.","When the patient says that he/she will look for another pharmacist, say that this is his/her right. State that you are very concerned about the client\u0027s well-being and try to persuade him/her to see a doctor urgently."]

ScenarioTitle: You are assisting a 26-year-old who admits to dieting despite being underweight.
Background: You are assisting a 26-year-old who admits to dieting despite being underweight. He/she is going to be on television in four weeks and wants to lose two more kilograms because he/she believes the television makes people look larger than they actually are. The client wants meal replacements or diet tablets so he/she will look good.
TasksJson: ["Explain that meal replacements (or tablets) are not a healthy way to lose weight and highlight that a balanced healthy diet is always preferable.","Empathise with the patient, but inform him/her that weight loss from diet tablets only works for a short period of time.","Recommend supplements for the client (e.g., iron tablets, calcium, etc.).","Suggest he/she seek a dietitian\u0027s advice."]

ScenarioTitle: Your client has come in complaining of sneezing (often), runny nose, and itchy, puffy, watery and red eyes.
Background: Your client has come in complaining of sneezing (often), runny nose, and itchy, puffy, watery and red eyes. He/she has painful sinuses. He/she has experienced hay fever (allergic rhinitis) every year at this time. The client has used antihistamine tablets for years, but he/she thinks they no longer work.
TasksJson: ["Explain that the client should try a different antihistamine and suggest that changing the brand or type (e.g., Telfast: fexofenadine, Clarityne: loratadine) may see a change in the effectiveness of the drug.","Answer the client\u0027s questions about non-drowsy antihistamines but caution that he/she should test his/her reaction before driving.","Suggest paracetamol to relieve sinus pain. Explain not to use a nasal spray to avoid a rebound effect. If the sinus is very painful, suggest steam inhalation.","Suggest the use of a preventive medicine (e.g., a steroid nose spray), starting prior to the allergy season (may take a couple of days to work).","Make suggestions to help prevent future attacks (e.g., keep windows in the house and cars closed during pollen season, remove plants that trigger hay fever from the garden, etc.)."]

ScenarioTitle: A client has come in to the pharmacy with large transparent medical adhesive tape securing a dressing on his/her left shoulder following the
Background: A client has come in to the pharmacy with large transparent medical adhesive tape securing a dressing on his/her left shoulder following the excision of an elevated mole (papule). He/she believes that the wound may be infected as it is itchy and sore. On examination, you discover evidence of an allergic contact dermatitis the shape and size of the adhesive tape.

ScenarioTitle: A regular client comes into the pharmacy complaining that his/her heartburn (a chronic problem) appears to be getting worse, and that he/she
Background: A regular client comes into the pharmacy complaining that his/her heartburn (a chronic problem) appears to be getting worse, and that he/she is experiencing extreme indigestive discomfort. The patient hates seeing doctors, and wants you to provide something for the discomfort. You have concerns that the symptoms may be due to more serious problems.
TasksJson: ["Ask about recent symptoms. Explain that sometimes other problems can mimic indigestion \u2014 tactfully give examples (e.g., heart rhythm disturbances, heart failure, heart attack, side effects from medication, etc.).","Outline the tests a doctor might recommend to diagnose the cause (e.g., a stress test for the heart, breath test for H. pylori stomach ulceration, endoscopy, etc.).","When the patient asks for medication, point out that none of the usual non-prescription medications for indigestion are likely to help and explain how they could be dangerous in an undiagnosed situation.","When the patient says that he/she will look for another pharmacist, say that this is his/her right. State that you are very concerned about the client\u0027s well-being and try to persuade him/her to see a doctor urgently."]

ScenarioTitle: A 61-year-old patient is awaiting surgery for a fractured wrist and ankle.
Background: A 61-year-old patient is awaiting surgery for a fractured wrist and ankle. He/she has noticed that their regular medication has been changed and wants to discuss it with you.
TasksJson: ["Confirm reason for seeing patient (discussion of medication: temporary changes, routine procedure, etc.). Find out about any concerns (specific medications, reasons for change, etc.)","Explain medications are being withheld to reduce surgical risks (e.g., prevention of blood pressure drop, prevention of bleeding during surgery, etc.).","Emphasise one medication to be swapped (e.g., apixaban replaced with dalteparin, etc.). Stress regular medication will be restarted once he/she is stable post-surgery (e.g., vital signs in normal range, ready for discharge, etc.).","Reassure patient there is no risk (e.g. short timescale, standard procedure, etc.). Explore reasons for his/her anxiety (e.g., negative experiences, historical compliance, etc.).","Stress new medication is safest for surgery (dalteparin: lower risk of bleeding, bleeding easier to manage, etc.) Reassure him/her about side effects (rare: drop in platelet counts, changes in liver function, easy to screen for etc.)."]

Background: You are talking to James Sutton, a 50 year old worker after a workplace health check identified that he has high cholesterol and high blood pressure. The patient has been prescribed statins , but is unsure about taking them.
TasksJson: ["1. Find out as much as you can about what the patient knows about his condition.","2. Explain the risks of high cholesterol and high blood pressure \u2013 talk about heart attack and stroke.","3. Explain how statins work and advise about side effects.","4. Advise how to take the tablets (take with breakfast, take whole without chewing, keep in a cool place"]

ScenarioTitle: Your client has come in complaining of sneezing (often), runny nose, and itchy, puffy, watery and red eyes.
Background: Your client has come in complaining of sneezing (often), runny nose, and itchy, puffy, watery and red eyes. He/she has painful sinuses. He/she has experienced hay fever (allergic rhinitis) every year at this time. The client has used antihistamine tablets for years, but he/she thinks they no longer work.
TasksJson: ["Explain that the client should try a different antihistamine and suggest that changing the brand or type (e.g., Telfast: fexofenadine, Clarityne: loratadine) may see a change in the effectiveness of the drug.","Answer the client\u0027s questions about non-drowsy antihistamines but caution that he/she should test his/her reaction before driving.","Suggest paracetamol to relieve sinus pain. Explain not to use a nasal spray to avoid a rebound effect. If the sinus is very painful, suggest steam inhalation.","Suggest the use of a preventive medicine (e.g., a steroid nose spray), starting prior to the allergy season (may take a couple of days to work).","Make suggestions to help prevent future attacks (e.g., keep windows in the house and cars closed during pollen season, remove plants that trigger hay fever from the garden, etc.)."]

ScenarioTitle: This client has come to pick up a newly filled prescription for blood pressure medications.
Background: This client has come to pick up a newly filled prescription for blood pressure medications. You notice that he/she hasn't obtained a new supply of eye drops to treat his/her glaucoma for several months. You know that the eye drops should be replaced each month to make sure that they remain effective and to prevent any risk of the bottle becoming contaminated with bacteria/viruses.
TasksJson: ["Find out why the patient hasn\u0027t had his/her eye drops replaced in several months.","Explain the importance of discarding the eye drops each month and replacing them with a new bottle, even if there is still some medication left.","Persuade the patient to have a new bottle dispensed today and to bring the old bottle back to the pharmacy to be discarded."]

ScenarioTitle: A client visits the pharmacy wanting advice on treatment for head lice.
Background: A client visits the pharmacy wanting advice on treatment for head lice. He/she has a child at home suffering with itchy scalp, and when the hair was checked, eggs and lice were found in the child's hair. He/she wants you to recommend treatment for the condition.
TasksJson: ["Ask the client to explain the child\u0027s condition.","Reassure the client that head lice in children attending kindergarten and school is quite common.","Explain that you have a number of treatments on the shelf and that he/she should read and follow the directions carefully.","Explain the wet combing method using conditioner (requires a lot of patience) if non-insecticide based product is insisted upon.","Explain ways to prevent re-infestation (e.g., tying hair back, avoiding sharing hair brushes, checking head weekly, etc.).","Explain the importance of the client washing the bed linen in 60 degree water or dry in dryer on hot cycle for 20 minutes."]

ScenarioTitle: This 34-year-old client thinks he/she may have a peptic ulcer and has come to your pharmacy to request Prilosec (omeprazole), an over-the-co
Background: This 34-year-old client thinks he/she may have a peptic ulcer and has come to your pharmacy to request Prilosec (omeprazole), an over-the-counter proton pump inhibitor. You need to establish whether this medication would be suitable for the client.
TasksJson: ["Ask about the client\u0027s history with this medication, diagnosis and symptoms.","Explain that the client\u0027s condition is more likely to be gastric reflux.","Give the client information about the condition (e.g., more common than peptic ulcer, results from acid stomach contents rising upwards from stomach, etc.).","Ensure the client is not experiencing blood in vomit or bowel motions or taking any blood thinning medications (e.g., aspirin, etc.).","Recommend antacid medication and encourage the client to see a doctor if the medicine does not relieve the symptoms, or if the episodes become more frequent (e.g., may require further investigation and/or prescription medication, etc.)."]

ScenarioTitle: A 53-year-old client has come to the pharmacy to collect their regular prescription, ranitidine, for heartburn and acid reflux.
Background: A 53-year-old client has come to the pharmacy to collect their regular prescription, ranitidine, for heartburn and acid reflux. It is currently unavailable, due to a global manufacturing shortage.
TasksJson: ["Find out reason for client\u0027s visit.","Explain ranitidine is unavailable (global manufacturing shortage, alternatives only for foreseeable future, etc). Offer omeprazole as alternative (e.g., popular, safe medication, few side effects etc).","Offer over-the-counter/OTC famotidine (e.g., very similar to ranitidine, unlikely to cause diarrhoea, etc.).","Stress you will not be able to dispense ranitidine for the foreseeable future (e.g., unavailable, out of stock in all pharmacies etc.). Find out about his/her specific concerns (e.g., unplanned change to medication, side effects, etc.).","Reassure client that famotidine is a good option (e.g., unlikely to produce side effects; visit doctor if any occur; safely available as OTC medication; available to purchase now; etc.). Establish client\u0027s willingness to start taking famotidine."]

ScenarioTitle: The client has come to collect a script for tramadol, a strong pain-relieving tablet.
Background: The client has come to collect a script for tramadol, a strong pain-relieving tablet. He/she also asks for a bottle of St John's wort (Hypericum perforatum), a herbal preparation that may help with depression. The client has been taking the tramadol regularly for severe back pain; he/she has been experiencing a low mood for some time.
TasksJson: ["Find out why the client wants to buy St John\u0027s wort, and what he/she knows about it.","Explain that it would be dangerous to mix the herbal treatment with strong pain-relieving medication. There is an interaction between tramadol and St John\u0027s wort that could lead to a serious reaction (e.g., tremors, seizures, possible death, etc.).","Answer any questions, and make sure that the client understands why you strongly advise against buying the herbal antidepressant.","Persuade the client to visit his/her doctor to discuss the low moods and possible treatment options, including non-drug treatments."]

ScenarioTitle: Your client is a 42-year-old retail marketing manager who has a five-year history of mild irritable bowel syndrome (IBS).
Background: Your client is a 42-year-old retail marketing manager who has a five-year history of mild irritable bowel syndrome (IBS). In the last month, the client has experienced symptoms of diarrhoea, abdominal bloating and nausea, which are more severe than usual. The client has recently moved house and commenced a new job. He/she requests medication to relieve the nausea and diarrhoea. The client is worried about the condition becoming worse and seeks your advice on the management of IBS.
TasksJson: ["Reassure the client that the condition can be managed (e.g., De-Gas or peppermint oil: relief of bloating; loperamide: antidiarrhoeal, etc.).","Explain that stress factors (e.g., moving house, new job, etc.) may exacerbate IBS.","Stress the importance of diet and lifestyle in minimising symptoms (e.g., low-fat, low-sugar, high-fibre diet) and for long-term management (e.g., loperamide can only be used short-term).","Encourage the client to see a doctor if symptoms persist."]

ScenarioTitle: Your client has a 5-year-old son who recently commenced antibiotics for a chest infection.
Background: Your client has a 5-year-old son who recently commenced antibiotics for a chest infection. A rash has appeared on his right arm (two ring-shaped lesions, one the size of a coin, the other 5cm diameter). You recognise the rash as ringworm but your client is worried the rash is due to an allergic reaction to antibiotics.
TasksJson: ["Explain that the diagnosis is not a reaction to antibiotics but ringworm.","Answer the client\u0027s question about whether or not to stop giving antibiotics to his/her son.","Give information about ringworm (e.g., a fungal infection; will resolve in 2-4 weeks; use topical ointment; take care of personal hygiene, etc.).","Reassure the client that there are no signs of a serious allergic reaction (e.g., difficulty breathing, dizziness, swollen throat/tongue, etc.).","Explain that it is important to complete the course of antibiotics and advise him/her to consult the doctor if the rash persists after two weeks of treatment."]

ScenarioTitle: This 42-year-old reports a mild, but annoying headache which started today.
Background: This 42-year-old reports a mild, but annoying headache which started today. In the past 24 hours, he/she has stopped consuming tea, coffee, cola and chocolate, after reading that caffeine is bad for health. He/she seems anxious.
TasksJson: ["Explain that headaches are a common consequence of stopping drinking tea or coffee (i.e., caffeine withdrawal).","Recommend possible courses of action (e.g., taking over-the-counter painkillers to reduce headache symptoms, reducing the amount of caffeine gradually, maintaining overall fluid intake, waiting for the symptoms to pass in 2-3 days, etc.).","Reassure the client that a more serious cause is unlikely. Explain when to see a doctor (e.g., if the headache persists for more than 24 hours after starting painkillers; problems with balance; visual disturbances; memory loss; fever; joint or muscle pain, etc.)."]

ScenarioTitle: This client has come to the pharmacy with a prescription for dicloxacillin (a penicillin antibiotic) to treat a skin infection on his/her ri
Background: This client has come to the pharmacy with a prescription for dicloxacillin (a penicillin antibiotic) to treat a skin infection on his/her right leg. Whilst discussing the medication, you discover that the client is allergic to penicillins. Last time this client had amoxicillin (another penicillin antibiotic), he/she experienced an itchy rash all over the body. You think the prescribing doctor is probably unaware of the allergy, and that the client should go back to discuss it.
TasksJson: ["Ask the client about his/her previous allergic reactions to medication, including penicillin.","Ask if the client has recently changed doctors. If so, has the new doctor been told about the previous allergic reaction to penicillin?","Explain that dicloxacillin and amoxicillin are both penicillins, and it is therefore highly likely that the client will be allergic to both.","Be tactful, but persuade the client to return to the doctor for another consultation. Explain that there are other suitable antibiotics such as cefalexin which could be used to treat this skin infection."]

ScenarioTitle: You have a parent whose 16-year-old son developed a rash on his arm when climbing a tree, probably due to sap.
Background: You have a parent whose 16-year-old son developed a rash on his arm when climbing a tree, probably due to sap. He developed a rash that is red with small blister-like lumps and swelling. You believe the son has contact eczema.
TasksJson: ["Find out what the parent has done to treat the rash.","Reassure the parent that bathing the area was the right treatment to remove residual sap.","Explain that contact eczema is different to the atopic eczema experienced as a baby. Atopic eczema usually improves by the age of four and if it reappears will usually be on the eyelids, neck and wrist.","Explain that a moisturizing product with no fragrances should be applied. The parent can also apply thin cloths dipped in water to the lesions for 30 minutes \u2013 four to six times a day. After the blisters have subsided, a topical corticosteroid would usually be applied, e.g., Hydrocortisone 1% ointment if itching persists (very weak, short term treatment is safe)."]

Background: A 58-year-old patient, who is three weeks post-heart attack, was prescribed bisoprolol upon discharge. He/she is now concerned about the side effects of this medication.
TasksJson: ["Find out reason for client\u0027s visit.","Outline most common side effects of bisoprolol (e.g., bradycardia, low mood, fatigue, dyspnoea, etc.). Find out how he/she is managing his/her medication (compliance, etc.).","Explore his/her reasons for wanting a lower dose (e.g., side effects, information received, etc.). Explain dose depends on individual client (e.g., recovery rate, doctor\u0027s assessment etc.).","Reassure client fatigue is normal post-heart attack (e.g., to improve with time, etc.). Stress importance of continuing medication at current dose (e.g., reduction in risk of future heart attacks, following doctor\u0027s prescription/advice etc.).","Emphasise inability to dispense lower dose without prescription (e.g., risk to client\u0027s safety, pharmacists must follow protocol, etc.). Suggest appointment with his/her doctor (e.g., discussion of specific problems, adapting dose etc.)."]

Background: A 74-year-old client has been told to gradually reduce the dose of their medication, amiodarone, to control arrhythmia (irregular heartbeat). He/she is finding this complicated to manage.
TasksJson: ["Find out about client\u0027s medication (name, reason for prescription, etc.). Explore his/her understanding of reduction in dosage (reasons for, method, instructions, etc.).","Explain how to reduce dose (e.g., week 1: 200mg tablet, three per day; week 2: 2 tablets per day; week 3: 1 tablet per day, final dose, etc.). Background: This client has come to the pharmacy with a prescription for dicloxacillin (a penicillin antibiotic) to treat a skin infection on his/her right leg. Background: A regular client comes into the pharmacy complaining that his/her heartburn (a chronic problem) appears to be getting worse, and that he/she is experiencing extreme indigestive discomfort. ScenarioTitle: The client visits your pharmacy complaining that he/she has a flat, red, ring-shaped sore on his/her hand.
Background: The client visits your pharmacy complaining that he/she has a flat, red, ring-shaped sore on his/her hand. He/she tells you that he/she has been treating it with antiseptic cream, but it hasn't healed. You inspect the lesion and see that it is ringworm.
TasksJson: ["Ask the client to explain his/her condition and the treatment.","Explain to the client that he/she has ringworm and it needs an antifungal cream to treat it.","Reassure the client that ringworm is a common condition and anyone can get it. TasksJson: ["Explain that rest and plenty of fluids are essential. The condition has nothing to do with worms.","Tell him/her with correct treatment it will go away, but that in the mean time it is highly contagious. Provide suggestions on preventing from spreading the infection (e.g., do not share clothing/towels, etc.)."]

ScenarioTitle: A patient asks for advice about her acne. She has already tried cleansers and spot treatments, but they haven't made a difference.
Background: A patient asks for advice about her acne. She has already tried cleansers and spot treatments, but they haven't made a difference. She is embarrassed about her appearance and keen to find a treatment which will control the skin problem.
TasksJson: ["1. Ask the patient to explain a bit more about her acne and the treatment she\u0027s used.","2. Ask for more information about how the patient used the cream.","3. Explain that the cream may not have been used correctly, causing the skin reaction. Advise that antibiotics and the oral contraceptive pill may also be prescribed.","4. Explain the possible side effect of photosensitivity when taking doxycycline.","5. Give general advice on the management of whiteheads \u2013 speak to GP for further treatment, keep skin clean, use cream on clean, dry skin and avoid touching face."]

ScenarioTitle: A regular client comes into the pharmacy complaining that his/her heartburn (a chronic problem) appears to be getting worse, and that he/she
Background: A regular client comes into the pharmacy complaining that his/her heartburn (a chronic problem) appears to be getting worse, and that he/she is experiencing extreme indigestive discomfort. The patient hates seeing doctors, and wants you to provide something for the discomfort. You have concerns that the symptoms may be due to more serious problems.
TasksJson: ["Ask about recent symptoms. Explain that sometimes other problems can mimic indigestion \u2014 tactfully give examples (e.g., heart rhythm disturbances, heart failure, heart attack, side effects from medication, etc.).","Outline the tests a doctor might recommend to diagnose the cause (e.g., a stress test for the heart, breath test for H. pylori stomach ulceration, endoscopy, etc.).","When the patient asks for medication, point out that none of the usual non-prescription medications for indigestion are likely to help and explain how they could be dangerous in an undiagnosed situation.","When the patient says that he/she will look for another pharmacist, say that this is his/her right. State that you are very concerned about the client\u0027s well-being and try to persuade him/her to see a doctor urgently."]

ScenarioTitle: A 53-year-old client has come to the pharmacy to collect their regular prescription, ranitidine, for heartburn and acid reflux.
Background: A 53-year-old client has come to the pharmacy to collect their regular prescription, ranitidine, for heartburn and acid reflux. It is currently unavailable, due to a global manufacturing shortage.
TasksJson: ["Find out reason for client\u0027s visit.","Explain ranitidine is unavailable (global manufacturing shortage, alternatives only for foreseeable future, etc). Offer omeprazole as alternative (e.g., popular, safe medication, few side effects etc).","Offer over-the-counter/OTC famotidine (e.g., very similar to ranitidine, unlikely to cause diarrhoea, etc.).","Stress you will not be able to dispense ranitidine for the foreseeable future (e.g., unavailable, out of stock in all pharmacies etc.). Find out about his/her specific concerns (e.g., unplanned change to medication, side effects, etc.).","Reassure client that famotidine is a good option (e.g., unlikely to produce side effects; visit doctor if any occur; safely available as OTC medication; available to purchase now; etc.). Establish client\u0027s willingness to start taking famotidine."]

ScenarioTitle: Your client has a flu and is complaining of a sore throat, blocked nose and headache.
Background: Your client has a flu and is complaining of a sore throat, blocked nose and headache. The client has a fever of 38°C, and is feeling hot and cold. He/she has aching muscles, joints and has a cough.
TasksJson: ["Explain that rest and plenty of fluids are essential. You understand that work is important, but make it clear that feeling so unwell and work involving driving can be dangerous.","Explain that the flu virus will get worse before it gets better as the body\u0027s immune system fights the virus. White or slightly yellow mucus may develop or if symptoms worsen, yellow or green mucus may develop.","Suggest bed rest, fluids and paracetamol. Lozenges are a good idea and nasal spray may be used for a few days to avoid rebound congestion.","Emphasise there are no quick remedies and rest is best advisable. If symptoms persist go to the doctor."]

ScenarioTitle: This 34-year-old client thinks he/she may have a peptic ulcer and has come to your pharmacy to request Prilosec (omeprazole), an over-the-co
Background: This 34-year-old client thinks he/she may have a peptic ulcer and has come to your pharmacy to request Prilosec (omeprazole), an over-the-counter proton pump inhibitor. You need to establish whether this medication would be suitable for the client.
TasksJson: ["Ask about the client\u0027s history with this medication, diagnosis and symptoms.","Explain that the client\u0027s condition is more likely to be gastric reflux.","Give the client information about the condition (e.g., more common than peptic ulcer, results from acid stomach contents rising upwards from stomach, etc.).","Ensure the client is not experiencing blood in vomit or bowel motions or taking any blood thinning medications (e.g., aspirin, etc.).","Recommend antacid medication and encourage the client to see a doctor if the medicine does not relieve the symptoms, or if the episodes become more frequent (e.g., may require further investigation and/or prescription medication, etc.)."]

ScenarioTitle: A client has come in to the pharmacy with large transparent medical adhesive tape securing a dressing on his/her left shoulder following the
Background: A client has come in to the pharmacy with large transparent medical adhesive tape securing a dressing on his/her left shoulder following the excision of an elevated mole (papule). TasksJson: ["Explain to the client that there is no evidence of infection, but there is evidence of a skin reaction to the adhesive tape (quite common).","Advise immediate removal of the tape and using mild soap and water to clean the area which had tape on it.","Explain that there are no alternative adhesive tapes but recommend securing the dressing with a bandage instead.","Assure him/her that the hypoallergenic bandages are quite safe.","Discuss ways to shower without getting the bandage wet until it is removed (e.g., cover with plastic wrap, buy a bandage cover, etc.).","Answer his/her questions about signs of infection (e.g., fever, nausea, etc.)."]

ScenarioTitle: You are assisting a 26-year-old who admits to dieting despite being underweight.
Background: You are assisting a 26-year-old who admits to dieting despite being underweight. He/she is going to be on television in four weeks and wants to lose two more kilograms because he/she believes the television makes people look larger than they actually are. The client wants meal replacements or diet tablets so he/she will look good.
TasksJson: ["Explain that meal replacements (or tablets) are not a healthy way to lose weight and highlight that a balanced healthy diet is always preferable.","Empathise with the patient, but inform him/her that weight loss from diet tablets only works for a short period of time.","Recommend supplements for the client (e.g., iron tablets, calcium, etc.).","Suggest he/she seek a dietitian\u0027s advice."]

ScenarioTitle: You are speaking to a 30-year-old client who has come to talk to you about a rash that they have recently noticed.
Background: You are speaking to a 30-year-old client who has come to talk to you about a rash that they have recently noticed.
TasksJson: ["Find out how they first noticed rash (onset, location, etc.). Explore how it has developed (appearance, spread, sensation etc.).","Explore client\u0027s management of rash (e.g., creams, dressings, bathing, etc.). Explore possible causes of rash (allergies, environment, new medication etc.).","Find out about client\u0027s new medication (name, reasons for prescription, how long taken for, dose, etc.). Explore whether he/she has experienced flu-like symptoms since starting medication (fever, cough, headache etc.).","Reassure client rash is unlikely to be serious (e.g., common side effect of lamotrigine, etc.). Stress need to stop using lamotrigine (e.g., precautionary measure, need to rule out serious side effects etc.). Establish client\u0027s willing to make appointment with doctor (e.g., ability to book and attend an immediate appointment etc.)."]

Background: This client has come in to the pharmacy with a cut on the leg that he/she sustained a few days ago, when he/she scraped against some coral while diving. However, he/she is reluctant to do so.

ScenarioTitle: Your client has a 5-year-old son who recently commenced antibiotics for a chest infection.
Background: Your client has a 5-year-old son who recently commenced antibiotics for a chest infection. A rash has appeared on his right arm (two ring-shaped lesions, one the size of a coin, the other 5cm diameter). You recognise the rash as ringworm but your client is worried the rash is due to an allergic reaction to antibiotics.
TasksJson: ["Explain that the diagnosis is not a reaction to antibiotics but ringworm.","Answer the client\u0027s question about whether or not to stop giving antibiotics to his/her son.","Give information about ringworm (e.g., a fungal infection; will resolve in 2-4 weeks; use topical ointment; take care of personal hygiene, etc.).","Reassure the client that there are no signs of a serious allergic reaction (e.g., difficulty breathing, dizziness, swollen throat/tongue, etc.).","Explain that it is important to complete the course of antibiotics and advise him/her to consult the doctor if the rash persists after two weeks of treatment."]

ScenarioTitle: You see a 60-year-old client who has recently been prescribed warfarin to treat a blood clot.
Background: You see a 60-year-old client who has recently been prescribed warfarin to treat a blood clot. He/she has come to the pharmacy to collect a prescription of the medication.
TasksJson: ["Find out reason for client\u0027s visit.","Find out relevant client details (if first warfarin prescription, any other medication, knowledge of: dose, timing, side effects, etc.).","Emphasise importance of discussion before dispensing medication (e.g., ensuring understanding of dosage/side effects, checking for contraindications, etc.). Give information about taking warfarin (e.g., one dose each evening, regular time, etc.). Describe possible side effects (e.g., bleeding/bruising more easily, etc.).","Advise of action if dose missed/forgotten (e.g., take dose as soon as possible, maximum one dose each day, etc.). Make suggestions for remembering medication (e.g., alarm on phone, dosette box, etc.). Remind client of need for regular blood tests (e.g., monitoring international normalised ratio/INR, establishing correct ongoing dosage, etc.). Find out if client has appointment for first blood test.","Warn client about cessation of warfarin (e.g., only before procedures with risk of bleeding, decision by doctor/dentist, etc.). Find out any further questions or concerns."]

ScenarioTitle: Your patient is 49 years old, overweight and has recently been diagnosed with emphysema, which causes breathlessness, increased phlegm and c
Background: Your patient is 49 years old, overweight and has recently been diagnosed with emphysema, which causes breathlessness, increased phlegm and coughing. He/she has been smoking for 30 years. The doctor has referred the patient for physiotherapy to help manage the condition.
TasksJson: ["Ask how much the patient smokes and when he/she experiences breathlessness.","Educate the patient about chronic pulmonary disease (lung condition involving shortness of breath, etc.) and how it can affect him/her (e.g., limits airflow to lungs, etc.).","Suggest exercises that will help to allow the lungs to work easier (e.g., lean against wall with arms folded above head, etc.).","Discuss ways to ease the coughing (e.g., sucking on ice, relaxed breathing, etc.).","Encourage the patient to work towards stopping smoking entirely."]

ScenarioTitle: You see Mr Gerald Hughes, a 68-year-old retired bus driver with bilateral knee osteoarthritis, referred for exercise advice and self-managem
Background: You see Mr Gerald Hughes, a 68-year-old retired bus driver with bilateral knee osteoarthritis, referred for exercise advice and self-management education. He has been resting as much as possible and has put on 12 kg since retirement two years ago.
TasksJson: ["Find out Mr Hughes\u0027 current pain levels, activity levels, and daily functional limitations (e.g., stairs, walking distance, morning stiffness, etc.).","Explore and address his belief that exercise will \u0027wear the cartilage away faster\u0027; explain the evidence-based role of exercise in managing knee osteoarthritis (e.g., strengthens supporting muscles, reduces pain, improves function, etc.).","Discuss a tailored exercise programme appropriate to his condition (e.g., type, frequency, progression of activity; low-impact options such as swimming, cycling, walking; specific strengthening exercises, etc.).","Sensitively raise the topic of weight management and its impact on knee pain (e.g., reduced load through joints, improved mobility, etc.); avoid being judgmental; explore his readiness to consider referral to a dietitian.","Agree a self-management plan with Mr Hughes; check his understanding; provide safety-netting advice (e.g., if joint becomes hot, swollen, or significantly more painful, seek review, etc.)."]

ScenarioTitle: You see Mr David Clarke, a 45-year-old secondary school teacher, referred by his GP with a six-week history of lower back pain that started
Background: You see Mr David Clarke, a 45-year-old secondary school teacher, referred by his GP with a six-week history of lower back pain that started after lifting boxes at home. He believes he has a 'slipped disc' and will need surgery. His wife has accompanied him but is not present for the consultation.
TasksJson: ["Find out Mr Clarke\u0027s main concerns and the impact of his back pain on his daily life and work (e.g., sitting tolerance, time off work, activities affected, etc.).","Explore what he already knows or believes about his condition; correct any significant misconceptions (e.g., explain that a \u0027slipped disc\u0027 rarely requires surgery and that his presentation is likely musculoskeletal, etc.).","Explain the importance of staying active (e.g., avoid prolonged bed rest; gentle movement aids recovery; complete rest is counterproductive, etc.). Introduce the concept of a graded home exercise programme.","Address his concern that exercise will worsen his pain; reassure him and explain the difference between \u0027hurt\u0027 and \u0027harm\u0027 (e.g., some discomfort during activity is expected and not dangerous, etc.).","Provide safety-netting advice (e.g., symptoms that require urgent review: bladder or bowel changes, leg weakness, severe worsening pain, etc.). Check his understanding and agree a plan for the next appointment."]

ScenarioTitle: This middle-aged patient was admitted to hospital following a cerebrovascular accident (CVA) that has resulted in hemiparesis.
Background: This middle-aged patient was admitted to hospital following a cerebrovascular accident (CVA) that has resulted in hemiparesis. Speech is possible, although slurred, and he/she is now able to sit and stand with assistance. There has been some return of function in the limbs. He/she is now in the rehabilitation ward and is ready to commence physiotherapy to restore as much function as possible. Because the CVA was not very dense, the prognosis is quite good.
TasksJson: ["Explain what happened to the patient and what this means.","Assure him/her that the prognosis is quite good.","Answer the patient\u0027s questions about the degree of recovery that can be expected.","Explain what the therapy will involve and for how long it will continue (e.g., mobilisation, etc.).","Outline the facilities that can be provided at home if necessary (e.g., handrails, ramps, etc.)."]

ScenarioTitle: You are visiting Mrs Joan Whitfield, an 80-year-old widow who lives alone, referred by her GP following two falls in the past three months (
Setting: Patient's home. Community physiotherapy falls prevention visit.
Background: You are visiting Mrs Joan Whitfield, an 80-year-old widow who lives alone, referred by her GP following two falls in the past three months (once in the bathroom, once on the stairs). She has had no serious injuries but is very shaken. Her daughter, who lives nearby, arranged the referral but is not present.
TasksJson: ["Find out the circumstances of Mrs Whitfield\u0027s recent falls (e.g., time of day, activity at time of fall, any dizziness or warning, footwear worn, environmental factors, etc.).","Explore the emotional impact of the falls on her daily activities and independence; acknowledge her feelings appropriately (e.g., fear of falling again, avoidance of activities, effect on confidence, etc.).","Explain the falls prevention programme (e.g., balance and strength training); address her belief that she should simply \u0027be more careful\u0027 rather than exercise; link exercise to maintaining independence.","Discuss home safety modifications (e.g., removing trip hazards, improving lighting, appropriate footwear, use of walking aid); address her reluctance to remove a sentimental rug; suggest referral to occupational therapy for a formal assessment.","Check her understanding of the agreed plan; ensure she knows how to access emergency help (e.g., personal alarm, emergency contacts); provide clear safety-netting advice (e.g., when to contact her GP)."]

ScenarioTitle: Mrs Patricia Owens, a 58-year-old retired nurse, is attending for her first physiotherapy appointment six weeks following right rotator cuff
Setting: Outpatient orthopaedic physiotherapy clinic. Post-operative follow-up.
Background: Mrs Patricia Owens, a 58-year-old retired nurse, is attending for her first physiotherapy appointment six weeks following right rotator cuff repair. She has been in a sling since surgery and has not performed the exercises given at discharge because she is afraid of damaging the repair. On examination, you have found that active shoulder elevation is limited to approximately 80 degrees, passive range is fuller but uncomfortable at end range, and rotator cuff strength is reduced — all of which is consistent with normal healing at this stage.
TasksJson: ["Find out Mrs Owens\u0027 current symptoms, pain levels, sleep, and functional limitations since her operation (e.g., difficulty dressing, washing her hair, night pain, use of the arm, etc.).","Explain that you need to assess the shoulder today by gently moving it and testing its strength; obtain her consent and reassure her that the assessment will not damage the surgical repair.","Explain your examination findings in plain language (e.g., movement is limited and the muscles are weaker than normal, but this is exactly what you would expect six weeks after surgery; the repair is healing as it should, etc.).","Link your findings to her rehabilitation programme (e.g., explain why gentle, progressive exercises are now safe and necessary; explain the \u0027hurt versus harm\u0027 principle; address her fear that movement will tear the repair, etc.).","Agree the goals for the next six weeks (e.g., restoring movement, then strength); advise on precautions and activity modifications; provide safety-netting (e.g., signs to report to her surgeon, etc.) and check her understanding."]

ScenarioTitle: Your patient is a 68-year-old widow/widower who lives alone and is on a waiting list for a hip replacement operation.
Background: Your patient is a 68-year-old widow/widower who lives alone and is on a waiting list for a hip replacement operation. He/she may have to wait for another 12 months. The surgeon has sent him/her for physiotherapy assessment and management. The patient has been prescribed non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs).
TasksJson: ["Reassure the patient that physiotherapy can help to ease the discomfort while waiting for the hip replacement operation.","Ask about activities that aggravate and ease the condition.","Find out about the patient\u0027s mobility (e.g., driving, walking to shops, public transport, showering, etc.) and needs at home (e.g., cleaning, cooking, etc.).","Explain how physiotherapy can help the patient to become more mobile.","Discuss the possibility of moving the patient into supported accommodation to ease the burden on the patient\u0027s family."]

ScenarioTitle: This 63-year-old office worker with cervical spondylosis (osteoarthritis of the neck) is experiencing restricted movement when turning the h
Background: This 63-year-old office worker with cervical spondylosis (osteoarthritis of the neck) is experiencing restricted movement when turning the head to the left and is waking frequently at night due to the pain. The doctor has prescribed medication for the inflammation and pain and referred the patient to you.
TasksJson: ["Find out about the patient\u0027s everyday tasks at work and neck positioning.","Suggest the patient avoid leaning forward and holding the phone between the neck and shoulders, and recommend better postural positioning.","Recommend the patient see an optometrist for his/her vision problems and use a headpiece for the phone.","Describe exercises to improve strength and mobility of the neck (e.g., looking up and down, side to side, etc.).","Encourage the patient to remain active.","Recommend something to help ease the patient\u0027s neck while sleeping (e.g., a cervical pillow, etc.)."]

ScenarioTitle: Mrs Sunita Patel, a 62-year-old retired teacher, is four weeks following an ischaemic stroke with residual right-sided weakness.
Setting: Inpatient stroke rehabilitation ward. Bedside physiotherapy session.
Background: Mrs Sunita Patel, a 62-year-old retired teacher, is four weeks following an ischaemic stroke with residual right-sided weakness. She is right-hand dominant, has been tearful since admission, and has not been completing her prescribed exercises. On examination, you have found reduced grip strength and limited active movement in the right hand and arm, with some preserved finger movement and intact but altered sensation — findings consistent with her expected recovery at four weeks post-stroke.
TasksJson: ["Introduce your role in her rehabilitation; find out her current concerns and why she has not been completing her exercises (e.g., did not understand them, felt hopeless, etc.).","Explain that you need to assess her arm and hand today by checking her grip, movement, and sensation; obtain her consent and sensitively address her embarrassment about being assessed on an open ward.","Explain your examination findings in plain language (e.g., the hand grip and arm movement are weaker than normal, but there is still movement and feeling, and this is what you would expect at this stage of recovery, etc.).","Link your findings to the importance of daily repetitive exercises; explain in simple terms how the brain can re-learn movement with practice (neuroplasticity); address her fear that she will never recover.","Involve her in setting realistic short-term goals (e.g., what she would like to achieve before discharge); discuss how family support can help; check her understanding and agree the plan."]
