Background: This elderly patient has had a fractured femur caused by being knocked down by a car. It was subsequently treated with ORIF (open reduction internal fixation). You have to assist him/her to learn to walk again, initially supported by a walking frame. He/she is finding it difficult, painful and exasperating. After discharge, the treatment will continue on a twice-weekly basis.
TasksJson: ["Be sympathetic but encourage the patient to continue with his/her recovery plan despite the pain.","Reassure him/her that both the pain and difficulty will diminish.","Answer any questions regarding the long-term prognosis and independent living (e.g., recovery time depends on the specific injury and may take months; physiotherapy is essential to regain mobility and strength, etc.).","Outline the physiotherapy routine both while he/she is in hospital and after discharge (e.g., stretching and flexing to increase range of movement progressing to simple weight-bearing exercises and gait training, etc.)."]

ScenarioTitle: A 28-year-old patient has presented with a knee injury that was sustained while skiing overseas.
Background: A 28-year-old patient has presented with a knee injury that was sustained while skiing overseas. He/she reports an audible pop, immediate swelling and tenderness, and a feeling of instability. You suspect a torn anterior cruciate ligament (ACL). You perform a medial-lateral grind test to rule out meniscus damage.
TasksJson: ["Find out how the injury was sustained.","Ask about locking or catching sensations to rule out meniscal tears.","Explain your diagnosis to the patient (e.g., a tear in the tissue which joins the thigh bone to the shin bone, etc.).","Reassure him/her about the likelihood of full recovery.","Give advice regarding appropriate treatment (e.g., rest, ice, compression, elevation, etc.).","Outline any exercises that may be useful now or at a later stage (e.g., exercises to strengthen the muscles around the knee, cycling on a stationary bicycle, etc.)."]

ScenarioTitle: You are seeing a 50-year-old kayaker and cyclist. The patient began to experience numbness in his/her left foot after riding on a different
Background: You are seeing a 50-year-old kayaker and cyclist. The patient began to experience numbness in his/her left foot after riding on a different bicycle for 40 kilometres. The patient believes the new bike is the cause of the numbness.
TasksJson: ["Find out if the patient is experiencing weakness or paralysis.","Ask if the patient has had problems with his/her back.","In simple terms, explain that a nerve root or spinal nerve injury can refer numbness to a distal area that it supplies, like the foot.","Give examples of other possible causes of numbness in the foot (e.g., Morton\u0027s neuroma, pressure on nerve between 2/3 or 3/4 toes, Tarsal Tunnel Syndrome, etc.).","Agree that the problem could be with the bike and give examples of how the bike could cause the numbness (e.g., positioning of seat/pedals/length of frame, position when riding, etc.).","Assure the patient that it is necessary to rule out other physical causes initially."]

ScenarioTitle: This 63-year-old office worker with cervical spondylosis (osteoarthritis of the neck) is experiencing restricted movement when turning the h
Background: This 63-year-old office worker with cervical spondylosis (osteoarthritis of the neck) is experiencing restricted movement when turning the head to the left and is waking frequently at night due to the pain. The doctor has prescribed medication for the inflammation and pain and referred the patient to you.
TasksJson: ["Find out about the patient\u0027s everyday tasks at work and neck positioning.","Suggest the patient avoid leaning forward and holding the phone between the neck and shoulders, and recommend better postural positioning.","Recommend the patient see an optometrist for his/her vision problems and use a headpiece for the phone.","Describe exercises to improve strength and mobility of the neck (e.g., looking up and down, side to side, etc.).","Encourage the patient to remain active.","Recommend something to help ease the patient\u0027s neck while sleeping (e.g., a cervical pillow, etc.)."]

ScenarioTitle: This patient hurt his/her left ankle yesterday while playing soccer.
Background: This patient hurt his/her left ankle yesterday while playing soccer. He/she turned suddenly and heard a snap. The ankle is swollen, red, bruised and painful. The patient is unable to bear weight on the left foot. He/she thinks it is a sprain. You suspect a fracture or break.
TasksJson: ["Find out how the injury occurred and what the patient did to alleviate the pain.","Discuss other injuries the patient may have had to the ankle and when they occurred (e.g., sprains, etc.).","Refer the patient for X-rays and explain why you are doing this.","Maintain that you cannot prescribe treatment until the X-rays are returned but suggest ways to alleviate the pain and swelling (e.g., rest, ice, etc.).","Explain the difference between treatment of a sprained ankle and treatment of a broken ankle (e.g., fracture requires immobilisation, recovery will take longer, etc.)."]

ScenarioTitle: You see a 44-year-old warehouse worker whose custom foot orthoses have been delayed by two weeks because the external laboratory required a
Background: You see a 44-year-old warehouse worker whose custom foot orthoses have been delayed by two weeks because the external laboratory required a remake. The patient's previous device has cracked, and their heel/arch pain has increased.
TasksJson: ["Acknowledge the patient\u0027s frustration and apologise for the inconvenience without becoming defensive. Allow the patient to explain the impact of the delay.","Clarify the current symptoms and check whether there are any new concerning features that require clinical reassessment.","Explain the reason for the delay honestly and briefly, including that the device needed to be remade to ensure the correct fit and function.","Give a clear, realistic update about the expected completion process. Avoid making promises that cannot be guaranteed.","Offer appropriate interim options to reduce symptoms until the new orthoses are available (e.g. temporary support/footwear advice/activity modification as suitable). Confirm the patient is satisfied with the immediate plan and knows how they will be updated."]

ScenarioTitle: You have just examined a 26-year-old patient with a recurrent ingrown left great toenail.
Background: You have just examined a 26-year-old patient with a recurrent ingrown left great toenail. The lateral nail edge is embedded in the skin with local tenderness and mild inflammation, but there is no spreading cellulitis or abscess.
TasksJson: ["Begin by thanking the patient for allowing you to examine the toe, then explain the examination findings in clear language.","Clarify the history of previous episodes and self-treatment. Explain why repeated deep trimming can worsen recurrence.","Explain that antibiotics are not automatically required when there is no spreading infection, and outline signs that would change that decision.","Discuss management options, including conservative care and partial nail avulsion under local anaesthetic for recurrent symptoms. Explain what the procedure involves and address concerns about the injection and nail appearance.","Explain expected recovery and practical advice about footwear/work. Check the patient\u0027s understanding, answer remaining concerns and establish willingness to proceed with the agreed plan."]

ScenarioTitle: You are reviewing a 39-year-old teacher with plantar heel pain.
Background: You are reviewing a 39-year-old teacher with plantar heel pain. At the previous appointment, you advised a programme of calf/plantar fascia stretching, activity modification and supportive footwear.
TasksJson: ["Review the current symptoms and compare them with the previous visit (pain pattern, severity, function, morning pain, impact of standing and walking).","Explore adherence to the previous plan and identify practical barriers to stretching, activity modification and appropriate footwear.","Explain that plantar heel pain often improves gradually and that inconsistent loading and support can cause symptoms to persist or recur.","Address the request for imaging. Explain when imaging may be useful and why it is not always needed when the clinical picture is typical and there are no concerning features.","Discuss realistic options for support, including footwear changes and whether an off-the-shelf or custom device is appropriate. Agree on a practical revised plan and timeframe for review."]

ScenarioTitle: You see a 58-year-old patient with type 2 diabetes who has been referred for bilateral foot numbness and a plantar callus under the right fo
Background: You see a 58-year-old patient with type 2 diabetes who has been referred for bilateral foot numbness and a plantar callus under the right forefoot.
TasksJson: ["Find out more about the numbness and tingling (onset, progression, pain, night symptoms, previous episodes) and ask about any skin breaks, swelling or discharge.","Explore relevant foot-care habits and footwear (walking barefoot, self-treatment of callus, shoe fit, previous podiatry review).","Explain in simple terms how diabetes can reduce sensation in the feet and why repeated pressure over a callus can become a problem if the skin breaks down.","Advise the patient not to cut or shave the callus at home. Explain that the hard skin can be managed safely in clinic and that footwear should reduce pressure and rubbing.","Give practical preventive advice (daily foot checks, suitable footwear, prompt review of cuts/blisters/redness). Reassure the patient while explaining why regular monitoring is important. Check understanding and agreement with the plan."]

ScenarioTitle: You are discussing discharge foot-care planning with a 67-year-old patient with diabetes.
Background: You are discussing discharge foot-care planning with a 67-year-old patient with diabetes. The patient was admitted with an infected plantar ulcer, which is now improving after treatment. You have reviewed the wound during the admission.
TasksJson: ["Acknowledge the patient\u0027s relief and concerns about recurrence. Confirm their understanding of the current wound status and why ongoing protection is needed.","Explain the purpose of the off-loading footwear and why reducing pressure on the ulcer is essential for healing, even if the shoe feels inconvenient.","Explore practical challenges at home (living alone, shopping, mobility) and discuss realistic ways to reduce unnecessary walking while maintaining independence.","Explain the dressing and follow-up arrangements in broad terms, including who will review the wound and the importance of attending appointments.","Explain warning signs requiring urgent review (increasing redness, swelling, heat, discharge, worsening pain or systemic illness). Check understanding and agree on the discharge foot-care plan."]

ScenarioTitle: You see a 34-year-old patient who has been referred for a CT scan of the abdomen to investigate ongoing pain.
Background: You see a 34-year-old patient who has been referred for a CT scan of the abdomen to investigate ongoing pain. The patient is concerned about exposure to radiation and is questioning whether the scan is necessary and safe.
TasksJson: ["Find out the patient\u2019s specific concerns and acknowledge that questions about radiation are very reasonable (e.g. many patients ask the same thing).","Explain in simple terms how radiation dose is managed (e.g. the lowest dose needed for a clear picture is always used, scans are justified and only performed when the benefit outweighs the small risk).","Explain why a CT has been chosen rather than another test (e.g. it shows this particular area in far greater detail; ultrasound or MRI may not give the same information for this problem). Reassure that the doctor has requested it for a good clinical reason.","Correct the patient\u2019s misconceptions (e.g. the radiation does not stay in or build up in the body; it passes through at the moment of the scan, so there is no risk to their children at home).","Address any remaining worries, check the patient\u2019s understanding and confirm their agreement to proceed."]

ScenarioTitle: You see a 58-year-old patient who is due to have a contrast-enhanced CT scan.
Background: You see a 58-year-old patient who is due to have a contrast-enhanced CT scan. The patient is anxious about the intravenous contrast injection and about the possibility of an adverse reaction.
TasksJson: ["Find out the patient\u2019s specific concerns and reassure them (e.g. contrast injections are performed very commonly and safely every day in the department).","Explain what the injection involves and why the contrast is needed (e.g. a small cannula in the arm, a brief sharp scratch; the dye helps blood vessels and organs show up clearly for a more accurate diagnosis).","Normalise the expected sensations (e.g. a warm flush spreading through the body and sometimes a metallic taste are completely normal, harmless, and pass within a minute).","Take a brief allergy history and reassure appropriately (e.g. childhood hay fever does not mean an allergy to the contrast); explain staff are fully trained and equipped to manage any reaction and will monitor them throughout.","Check the patient\u2019s understanding, answer remaining questions and obtain their agreement to proceed."]

ScenarioTitle: You see a 45-year-old office worker who has been referred for an MRI scan of the knee following a sports injury.
Background: You see a 45-year-old office worker who has been referred for an MRI scan of the knee following a sports injury. The patient is anxious about the procedure, having expressed a strong fear of enclosed spaces.
TasksJson: ["Find out how the patient is feeling and acknowledge their anxiety (e.g. reassure them their feelings are very common, take time, do not rush). Establish the specific cause of their worry.","Explain what the MRI involves (e.g. for a knee scan only the affected leg generally needs to enter the scanner, the head and chest remain outside, the loud knocking noise is normal, ear protection/headphones provided).","Reassure the patient about safety and control (e.g. a call buzzer in their hand, two-way intercom, staff watching at all times, the scan can be stopped at any point). Explain the magnet is safe and the scan is painless.","Outline how long the scan will take and the importance of keeping still for clear images (e.g. around twenty minutes, movement blurs the pictures).","Offer practical coping strategies (e.g. eye mask, slow steady breathing, listening to music) and establish the patient\u2019s willingness to proceed."]

ScenarioTitle: You have just completed a wrist X-ray on a 29-year-old patient who fell while playing football.
Background: You have just completed a wrist X-ray on a 29-year-old patient who fell while playing football. The patient is pressing you to tell them immediately whether the wrist is fractured.
TasksJson: ["Acknowledge the patient\u2019s anxiety and their wish to know the result quickly (e.g. show you understand it is a worrying and frustrating situation, especially with a match coming up).","Explain tactfully why you are not able to give a diagnosis (e.g. the images must be formally reviewed and reported by a doctor or radiologist; interpreting them for the patient is outside your professional role and is done this way for the patient\u2019s safety).","Reassure the patient about the process (e.g. the images are of good quality, the doctor has everything they need, and you will send them across for review straight away).","Explain the next steps and give a realistic timeframe (e.g. the treating doctor will call them through, usually within a short while, and will explain exactly what the X-ray shows and advise about the match).","Manage the patient\u2019s frustration calmly and confirm they are willing to wait to see the doctor."]

ScenarioTitle: You see a 52-year-old woman attending for her first screening mammogram.
Background: You see a 52-year-old woman attending for her first screening mammogram. She is embarrassed and anxious, and is particularly concerned that the procedure will be painful.
TasksJson: ["Find out how the patient is feeling and acknowledge her concerns (e.g. nervousness and embarrassment at a first mammogram are extremely common; reassure her).","Explain the procedure simply and respectfully (e.g. undress to the waist behind the curtain, gentle positioning against the machine, two pictures of each breast, only the two of you present, you will talk her through each step).","Explain honestly why compression is necessary (e.g. it gives a much clearer image and actually lowers the radiation dose; any discomfort lasts only a few seconds and it will not cause harm).","Explain how long the appointment takes and how results are given (e.g. about fifteen minutes; results are not given on the day but sent by letter, usually within a couple of weeks).","Reassure the patient, check her understanding and confirm she is happy to proceed."]

ScenarioTitle: You are discussing discharge communication planning with a 70-year-old patient who has mild expressive aphasia following a stroke and is ret
Background: You are discussing discharge communication planning with a 70-year-old patient who has mild expressive aphasia following a stroke and is returning home tomorrow.
TasksJson: ["Acknowledge the patient\u0027s progress and frustration and find out which communication situations are most difficult.","Explain that recovery can continue after discharge and that therapy and practice focus on functional communication.","Give strategies for word-finding and for managing conversations when the patient becomes tired or stuck.","Explain how family members can support communication without rushing, interrupting or finishing every sentence.","Discuss follow-up therapy and practical goals for home and social situations. Check understanding and confidence."]

ScenarioTitle: You are discussing augmentative communication with the parent of a six-year-old child who has significant communication difficulties.
Background: You are discussing augmentative communication with the parent of a six-year-old child who has significant communication difficulties. The parent is reluctant to try a picture-based system.
TasksJson: ["Invite the parent to explain their concerns and acknowledge that wanting spoken communication for their child is understandable.","Explain in simple terms how an augmentative communication system can reduce frustration and support communication while speech development continues.","Address the misconception that using pictures automatically prevents or replaces speech development.","Explain how the system can be introduced gradually and consistently across home and school.","Agree on a small trial with clear goals and review. Check the parent\u0027s understanding and willingness to proceed."]

ScenarioTitle: You have just completed a swallowing assessment on a 62-year-old patient recovering from a stroke who has been coughing during meals.
Background: You have just completed a swallowing assessment on a 62-year-old patient recovering from a stroke who has been coughing during meals.
TasksJson: ["Thank the patient for allowing you to complete the assessment and explain the main findings in clear, non-technical language.","Explain why coughing during swallowing needs to be managed and discuss the recommended swallowing strategies.","Address the patient\u0027s reluctance regarding modified drinks and acknowledge their concern about enjoyment of eating and drinking.","Explain that swallowing ability can improve with rehabilitation but needs ongoing review and individualised progression.","Check the patient\u0027s understanding and agreement with the initial management plan."]

ScenarioTitle: You are reviewing a 34-year-old teacher undergoing voice therapy for functional hoarseness.
Background: You are reviewing a 34-year-old teacher undergoing voice therapy for functional hoarseness. Symptoms improved initially but have worsened after reduced adherence and heavy voice use.
TasksJson: ["Review the current symptoms, voice demands and adherence to previous exercises and vocal hygiene advice.","Explore practical barriers at work and identify situations in which the patient is overusing or straining the voice.","Explain that improvement often depends on consistent technique and load management rather than a fixed number of sessions.","Address questions about stopping work and whispering, and provide appropriate voice-conservation strategies.","Agree on a realistic revised plan and timeframe for review. Check the patient\u0027s confidence in following it."]

ScenarioTitle: You see the parent of a three-year-old child presenting for an initial assessment because of limited spoken language.
Background: You see the parent of a three-year-old child presenting for an initial assessment because of limited spoken language. The parent is anxious about the cause and feels guilty.
TasksJson: ["Find out more about the child\u0027s communication, comprehension, gestures, play, hearing history, interaction and language environment.","Acknowledge the parent\u0027s concern and explain that limited speech can have different causes and cannot be diagnosed from one feature alone.","Address the parent\u0027s fear about autism sensitively and explain what additional information or referral may be considered if indicated.","Reassure the parent that blaming themselves is not helpful and give practical language-stimulation strategies for everyday routines.","Explain the next assessment steps and check the parent\u0027s understanding and questions."]

ScenarioTitle: You are reviewing the owner of a seven-year-old Labrador with recurrent pruritus.
Background: You are reviewing the owner of a seven-year-old Labrador with recurrent pruritus. The dog initially responded to treatment, but the symptoms returned after treatment stopped.
TasksJson: ["Review the dog\u0027s response to previous treatment and clarify the timing and pattern of recurrent symptoms.","Explore possible triggers and relevant associated signs (ears, paws, skin infections, diet changes, seasonal pattern).","Explain that recurrent allergic skin disease may require investigation and ongoing management rather than a single permanent cure.","Address concerns about repeated medication and explain how benefits, side effects and monitoring are considered.","Discuss possible dietary or environmental investigation and agree on the next step. Check the owner\u0027s understanding and willingness to proceed."]

ScenarioTitle: You have just examined a nine-year-old cat with a one-month history of polydipsia and polyuria, with mild weight loss.
Background: You have just examined a nine-year-old cat with a one-month history of polydipsia and polyuria, with mild weight loss. The examination is not diagnostic, so blood and urine testing is recommended.
TasksJson: ["Thank the owner for allowing you to examine Milo and explain the general findings without creating unnecessary alarm.","Clarify the history of drinking, urination, appetite, weight, behaviour and any previous medical problems.","Explain in simple terms why blood and urine tests are needed and what types of conditions they may help identify.","Address the owner\u0027s fears about kidney disease or diabetes, explaining that a diagnosis cannot be made from symptoms alone and that many conditions can be managed.","Explain the immediate testing plan and when results are likely to be discussed. Check consent and understanding."]

ScenarioTitle: You are discharging a six-year-old dog after overnight treatment for vomiting and dehydration.
Background: You are discharging a six-year-old dog after overnight treatment for vomiting and dehydration. The dog is now bright, hydrated and has tolerated small amounts of food.
TasksJson: ["Acknowledge the owner\u0027s relief and anxiety about recurrence and briefly summarise the dog\u0027s current condition.","Explain the feeding plan, including small amounts, gradual return to normal food and access to water as appropriate.","Explain any medication instructions and practical signs that would suggest recurrent dehydration or worsening illness.","Advise on temporary activity restriction and gradual return to normal exercise.","Explain when urgent review is needed (persistent vomiting, inability to keep water down, marked lethargy, blood, collapse). Check the owner\u0027s understanding."]

ScenarioTitle: You need to speak to the owner of a dog whose planned dental procedure has been delayed because an emergency patient required immediate trea
Background: You need to speak to the owner of a dog whose planned dental procedure has been delayed because an emergency patient required immediate treatment. The owner is angry and has work commitments.
TasksJson: ["Acknowledge the inconvenience and the impact on the owner\u0027s day. Apologise for the poor communication without becoming defensive.","Explain briefly why the emergency case had to take priority and reassure the owner that their dog is safe and being monitored.","Address concerns about fasting and explain how the team will manage this safely while the procedure is delayed.","Give the most realistic update possible, including alternatives if the owner cannot wait, without making promises you cannot guarantee.","Check that the owner understands the plan and knows how they will be updated."]

ScenarioTitle: You see the owner of a four-month-old kitten presenting for the first time with two days of diarrhoea.
Background: You see the owner of a four-month-old kitten presenting for the first time with two days of diarrhoea. The kitten is reported to remain bright, drinking and without vomiting or blood in the stool.
TasksJson: ["Find out more about the diarrhoea, appetite, drinking, vomiting, blood, activity, diet, vaccination/deworming and possible access to unsuitable food.","Explain common causes of short-term diarrhoea in young cats in simple language and why hydration and general condition are important.","Explain why antibiotics are not automatically required in a bright kitten without evidence of bacterial infection.","Give safe home-care advice about diet, water and monitoring, and outline warning signs that require prompt veterinary review.","Check the owner\u0027s understanding and agree on when to return if the symptoms do not settle."]
